# SettingsRenderer Call relationships

`src/betterdiscord/ui/settings.tsx` is not a standalone settings routing entry point. When reading this file, first treat it as a TSX module that groups existing modules, persisted state, and layout objects together. Earlier notes listed several declarations consecutively; on review, it became clear that this style could easily lead someone to mistake `drawerStates` for an instance field of `SettingsRenderer`, or to assume that `DiscordModules.Layout` participates in renderer initialization from the start of the file.

The first reference point in the file is on line 31:

```ts
const SettingsRenderer = new class SettingsRenderer {
```

Here, `SettingsRenderer` is the binding name for an instance of an anonymous class. It is the starting point for inspecting the settings/rendering-related code in this file, but do not skip the intervening code and link it directly to the later layout variables as a single function call. The available references only establish where these names appear in the same file; which specific methods lie between them still has to be determined by reading down through the class body and subsequent assignments.

Next, inspect the persisted state on line 38 separately:

```ts
const drawerStates: Partial<Record<string, Record<string, boolean>>> = JsonStore.get("misc", "drawerStates") || {};
```

This expression uses two levels of string indexing: the outer key corresponds to a set of drawer states, and the inner key corresponds to a boolean value. When `JsonStore.get("misc", "drawerStates")` obtains an existing record, it uses that record directly; it falls back to `{}` only when no record exists. Therefore, when investigating the initial expanded state, first distinguish between "drawerStates is not present in storage" and "the value for a specific key is false." The former is handled by the default object here; the latter is part of the state content that already exists.

Layout handling does not appear until line 81:

```ts
const layoutModuleRaw = DiscordModules.Layout;
const out: Partial<LayoutBuilder> = {};
```

`layoutModuleRaw` retains `DiscordModules.Layout`, while `out` initially starts with the empty result of a partial `LayoutBuilder`. Later locations can be traced through `match` on line 87, `outKey` on line 91, and `rootLayout` on line 110. The practical reading order is to first see what `match` retrieves, then see how that result affects `outKey`, and finally check which object `rootLayout` references when layout assembly is complete. This is more reliable than guessing the layout source from the import names.

The visible objects in the file are arranged as follows; this diagram shows the code-navigation order, not that every line represents a runtime call edge:

```text
src/betterdiscord/ui/settings.tsx
|
+-- line 31  SettingsRenderer
|
+-- line 38  drawerStates
|     `-- JsonStore.get("misc", "drawerStates") || {}
|
`-- line 81  layoutModuleRaw = DiscordModules.Layout
      |
      +-- line 83  out: Partial<LayoutBuilder>
      +-- line 87  match
      +-- line 91  outKey
      `-- line 110 rootLayout
```

Dependencies are better split out by purpose instead of being treated as one undifferentiated list of names. `React, {ReactDOM}` comes from `@modules/react`; `Settings` and the type `SettingsCollection` come from `@stores/settings`; the persisted drawer state uses `JsonStore`, provided by `@stores/json`. The file also imports `Filters`, `getByKeys`, `getLazy`, `getLazyByStrings`, and `getMangled` from `@webpack`. These lookup utilities indicate that the layout and settings objects may need to be retrieved from webpack modules, but the import list itself does not identify the field corresponding to each utility.

On review of this page, recast the originally parallel declarations into two sections: state reads first, layout assembly second. For further tracing, prioritize the assignment fragment for `out` and the locations where `rootLayout` is used; the callers of `SettingsRenderer`'s methods and the write-back location for `drawerStates` are still not covered in this record.

# Notes on Reading Plural Call Relationships

This page still uses `src/common/i18n.ts` as the entry point. It is not a list of locale files or an overview of formatting tools; when reading Plural, the entry file puts resources, defaults, common utilities, and logger objects together, making it easy to misremember a "visible import" as a "confirmed call chain." That is exactly how the draft ended up with an overly short path map.

The draft focused on names: start by tracing down from `Plural`, then go back to the utility functions. That approach is quick when inspecting a local implementation, but it does not distinguish where resources are imported from, where default content enters the flow, or whether the logger object serves only an adjacent branch. When the old page is referenced, people often use this map to skip the file header; this revision only fills in the objects that should be followed within this file, rather than turning it into a new localization standard.

The file header shows the following four dependency groups:

```ts
import Localizations from "@assets/locales";
import Default from "@assets/locales/en-us.json";
import {formatString, getNestedProp} from "@common/utils";
import Logger from "./logger";
```

Keep `Localizations` and `Default` separate. The former comes from `@assets/locales`, while the latter points directly to `@assets/locales/en-us.json`. They may both appear in the read path, but they are not two spellings for the same object. The old note's description of the default language file as "Plural's default result" was not precise; from this entry point, all that can be established initially is that the default resource is imported. Which branch actually reads it still has to be checked against the declarations and use sites in the file.

The utilities should not be collapsed into a single black box either. The name of `formatString` indicates formatting, while the name of `getNestedProp` indicates nested-property reads; both are imported together from `@common/utils`, but that does not mean every Plural path passes through both. After locating Plural-related declarations, first mark the utility names that actually occur in them, then go back and see where their arguments come from. Looking only at the import gives you candidate adjacency, not call order.

The simple diagram retained from the old note is below. It records the lookup route at the time and is no longer treated as a relationship conclusion:

```text
Plural name
  │
  ├─ Locate the declaration and its uses in src/common/i18n.ts
  │
  ├─ Inspect the local occurrences of formatString / getNestedProp
  │
  ├─ Review the reference locations for Localizations and Default
  │
  └─ Then check whether Logger falls in the same branch
```

The value of this diagram is limited to the order. Locating the declaration first avoids treating a resource import as the implementation; then finding the local occurrences of the two utilities shows whether they actually appear in the same block as Plural; resource references are checked afterward because the locale directory and `en-us.json` have different roles. Leaving `Logger` until last is not because it is less important, but because the file-header import alone still cannot tell us whether the logger belongs to the normal path, an error path, or another piece of adjacent logic.

One historical misreading is easy to make during review: seeing `Default` and treating it as the universal fallback for every lookup failure. This wording was once useful for explaining why the default language resource appears in the file header, but it conflates "the default resource was imported" with "a particular read has already used it." The old wording is kept here so that a later search that finds the early note does not mistake it for verified behavior.

The actual trace can be done in three short jumps from each occurrence of Plural. On the first jump, record only the resource names near local variables, parameters, and return values; on the second, look only at whether `formatString` and `getNestedProp` appear in the same condition or an adjacent expression; only on the third jump should you trace the specific read sites for `Localizations` and `Default`. If `Logger` appears along the way, record it as the diagnostic exit for that local section; do not casually fold it into the pluralization result path. These annotations let later readers retrace the same file without pulling the entire i18n module into scope because of a single import name.

`DOC-03` records the local relationship of appPath; both pages may start near the shared file, but do not add the result of tracing appPath here. The subject here is always the reading path around Plural in `src/common/i18n.ts`.

One unresolved point remains: the file header can establish dependency direction, but it cannot replace a block-by-block check of the branches around the Plural declaration. The next time pluralization needs to be changed, use the old simple diagram to find the entry; when the default resource, nested reads, or the logger are involved, annotate again from the actual occurrences rather than reusing the draft's claim that "utility functions are enough to explain all relationships."

# eslint.config Runtime Options

Older notes called `eslint.config.js` "the entry point for the lint runtime configuration." That wording is still useful for searching, but it conflates two things: the configuration written in the file and the layer that actually initiates lint. During review, I first read through the declarations in the file; the original wording should no longer be understood to mean that all runtime parameters are determined here.

The reading approach retained now starts with static configuration. After opening the file, first separate the top-level declarations by purpose: items written directly in the configuration are local choices; content brought in from elsewhere is a direct dependency; locations adjacent to failures or events are marked separately. The benefit of reading it this way is not to draw conclusions for the configuration, but to distinguish before making changes whether a change modifies the configuration content or changes how it obtains that content.

The old version interpreted "options" broadly, including the loading order and outer calls. The file itself did not later support that scope. `eslint.config.js` can explain how the configuration side is organized, but it does not automatically explain which parameters the caller uses to load it, nor can a single declaration determine whether a given failure reaches the desktop runtime. The old broad definition is not being removed because some people still use this title to return to the file for historical clues; when reading it, treat it as the navigation habit used at the time, not as the current runtime instructions.

For an actual follow-up, start with three places. First, the top-level structure, to confirm whether the modification target is a local item or imported content; second, the source of each direct dependency, to avoid attributing dependency changes to the rule itself; third, the locations adjacent to failures or events, recording whether they are still within the file's visible scope. If the issue has moved beyond these three places, do not continue guessing at the call chain in the configuration file.

One gap remains after the review: no complete mapping between the declarations in the file and the outer execution entry point was established here. It was inaccurate to previously describe this gap as "the configuration takes over the runtime options"; the safer historical record is that the configuration entry point provides a starting point for inspection, while the specific execution conditions still need to be confirmed on the loading side. title: Discord chunk queue capture decision

versions.body:
# Discord chunk queue capture decision

For this compatibility startup, we'll first treat Discord's chunk queue as the discovery entry point. Early in startup, we can't assume that later module queries are already available; if the queue is treated only as a normal `push` entry point, there is nowhere to revisit content that arrived before the entry point was taken over.

The decision is to keep a capture point: first retain the queue seen before takeover, then continue processing chunks that arrive later. This decision does not include lazy lookup, declaration filtering, or the addon lifecycle. They may all depend on discovery results, but they should not in turn determine when the queue is taken over.

Start investigating at `src/betterdiscord/modules/discordmodules.ts`. It imports `@webpack`'s `Filters`, `getBulkKeyed`, `getByKeys`, `getBySource`, `getByStrings`, and `getModule`, along with type declarations from `discord/modules`. This makes it a suitable starting point for investigating the area around module discovery; these imports alone do not establish that any one query function is responsible for queue takeover.

Two initial options:

- Replace only `push` going forward. Small implementation, but no processing path for the existing queue.
- Capture the existing queue first, then replace `push`. This adds a replay step at startup, but maintains continuity at the discovery entry point.

We'll use the second option. Still unconfirmed: whether all modules in the existing queue should participate in subsequent lookups immediately, or whether the only guarantee is that they won't be lost during takeover. Leave that distinction open until caller review, then decide.

# Discord chunk queue capture decision

The original wording, "keep one capture point," was too broad. After review, it should be split into two actions: retaining the pre-takeover queue reference, and leaving an opportunity to replay that existing content. The former is a startup-order issue; only the latter involves module discovery. Writing them as the same thing could lead later investigations to mistakenly assume that every query must wait for the same point in time.

## Old notes, retained here

Early notes say, "Once the queue is treated only as an ordinary `push` entry, there is nowhere to replay content that has already entered it." Keep this wording, but it is not enough to infer that "all old chunks should execute synchronously." At the time, the queue itself was not distinguished from module visibility after replay.

The decision from then still stands: the takeover action should not be triggered by lazy lookup or the addon lifecycle. If the startup path waits for a particular lazy query to occur first, the capture point becomes accidental; and the first batch of queries has no reason to bear the side effect of installing the discovery entry point. The boundary here is ordering, not any particular module name.

## September review

Revisiting it from `src/betterdiscord/modules/discordmodules.ts`, what can be confirmed directly is that it puts two kinds of things next to each other: on one side are the query utilities for `@webpack`; on the other is the type surface of `discord/modules`. The file also imports `memoize`. This adjacency is enough to explain why earlier investigations pointed here: runtime discovery and public module types meet at the same module layer.

But "pointing here" does not establish ownership. `RemoteModule`, `GetClientInfo`, `UserAgentInfo`, `Dispatcher`, `InviteActions`, `SimpleMarkdown`, and `ReactSpring` are all imported types; they do not prove that these objects take over the queue. Likewise, `getByKeys`, `getBySource`, `getByStrings`, and `getModule` are query mechanisms and should not be described as implementation details of queue capture.

This review ruled out an approach that looked convenient: first pass the current queue to a query function, then install a `push` wrapper alongside the query result. Its advantage is that it puts the entry point into the existing discovery code; its drawback is that queue takeover depends on the first query, and existing and subsequent content follow different paths. The decision is not to adopt it.

Another approach that was discussed was to wrap only `push`, treating the queue already in existence as pre-startup history. The rationale was to touch less of the early runtime state. It is not adopted either: the goal of the compatibility train is precisely for the discovery entry point to cover the queue formed before startup, not merely to observe loading that happens afterward.

## Current division of responsibilities

- The queue side is responsible for capturing content that already existed before takeover and continuing to observe `push` after takeover.
- The discovery side can consume module information that has already entered, but is not responsible for deciding when to install the queue wrapper.
- Lazy lookup remains a separate issue; whether it needs to be woken up is left to the design discussion for DOC-12, and is not decided here in advance.

This does not require parsing all modules into the same structure here. All that is needed is to ensure that existing and new content do not lose the opportunity to enter the discovery path because their takeover times differ.

## Review note

One counterexample from the review is worth recording: if the wrapper is already installed but pre-takeover content has not been fed back through processing, a later `push` can look completely normal, and the module query may also succeed afterward; the problem will only affect objects that depend on an earlier chunk. So testing the result "a new chunk can be seen" is not enough to establish that the capture strategy is correct.

Conversely, treating all existing content as tasks to execute immediately could also misstate "save the queue" as "force everything to run." The existing material provides no basis for this forced execution. The decision text should commit only to the capture and replay paths, not expand into an execution strategy.

## For the next review

`webpackRequire` is the search name carried forward. It should be used to locate relevant calls and entry points, and should not automatically be interpreted as a synonym for arbitrary webpack queries.

The exact order of module visibility during replay still needs to be confirmed, along with whether any caller relies only on events after the wrapper is installed. Until that is confirmed, do not treat "replay complete" as a signal that startup is complete.
versions.change_summary: Separate the capture and replay boundaries

# Discord chunk queue capture decision

This record has kept its original title because the discussion has always concerned the same startup gap: Discord has already built up a chunk queue, but the runtime discovery entry point has not yet taken over. The module queries, type surface, and deferred listeners added later have made the surrounding context more complex, but they do not change what needs to be answered here—what queue takeover must preserve, and what responsibilities it should not take on along the way.

The original entry point is still at `src/betterdiscord/modules/discordmodules.ts`. Earlier investigations would lead here from webpack, discord modules, and several query names. This path is useful because it places runtime queries and module types in adjacent maintenance locations; it is not a map of implementation ownership. The older assessments below have therefore been left in place: they explain some approaches that seemed reasonable but were later abandoned.

### 2023-04: Initial wording

The first version had only one concern: if only subsequent `push` were treated as input, the contents already placed in the queue before takeover would become startup history. The wording at the time was "first retain the queue seen before takeover, then continue processing chunks that arrive later".

The two options at the time were straightforward.

1. Handle only new `push`. The benefit is a focused change, with seemingly lower risk; the cost is that the old queue does not enter the same discovery path.
2. Capture the existing queue before takeover, then continue observing subsequent `push`. The benefit is continuity across the time boundary; the cost is that the order in which the existing contents are subsequently processed must be specified.

The second option was chosen. This choice was never intended to execute every piece of old content immediately, nor to make every query call wait for startup to complete. It simply rejects the idea that "entering the queue earlier" is a difference that can be ignored.

The first version left one question unresolved: whether all modules in the existing queue should immediately participate in subsequent lookups. There was no answer to that question at the time. Keeping it is more accurate than adding a blanket statement that "everything is available", because "preserved" and "already visible to the query layer" are not inherently equivalent.

### An attribution that was later overturned

An earlier draft attributed the problem to module queries themselves: since `getByKeys`, `getBySource`, `getByStrings`, and `getModule` were all nearby, it seemed sufficient to feed the queue contents into one of those query entry points. That line of reasoning no longer applies.

These names describe lookup methods, not when the queue is taken over. Looking up modules by key, source snippet, or string and "when to start observing the queue" are questions at two different levels. Putting the wrapping step into the first query would make startup behavior depend on what some caller happens to look up first; if there is no query, capture is not installed; if the query comes late, the old queue has already been handled under a different set of assumptions. This attribution was later withdrawn, and the original passage is kept here to avoid once again treating the discovery of API as a startup hook.

Also no longer used is the check that "as long as queries for new chunks work, capture is fine." It covers only input after takeover. What is really easy to miss is this: the wrapper is already in place, and newly arriving chunks are being observed, but the segment from before takeover has never entered the replay path. From the outside, it looks like an intermittent missing-module issue, but the actual issue is a break at the startup time boundary.

### Review notes alongside the file

A focused review of `src/betterdiscord/modules/discordmodules.ts` was subsequently conducted. The direct dependencies visible in the file include:

```ts
import {memoize} from "@common/utils";
import type {
    RemoteModule,
    GetClientInfo,
    UserAgentInfo,
    Dispatcher,
    InviteActions,
    SimpleMarkdown,
    ReactSpring
} from "discord/modules";
import {Filters, getBulkKeyed, getByKeys, getBySource, getByStrings, getModule} from "@webpack";
import type React from "react";
```

This material led to two small but important corrections.

First, the module layer deals with both runtime objects and the declaration surface. `RemoteModule`, `GetClientInfo`, `UserAgentInfo`, `Dispatcher`, `InviteActions`, `SimpleMarkdown`, and `ReactSpring` are type imports; they should not be used to prove that an object has already appeared during queue replay. Type names help with reading module interfaces; they are not evidence of queue-processing events.

Second, `Filters` and the various `get*` lookup tools can explain why the old records treated this location as an entry point for verification, but they cannot place responsibility for wrapping the queue directly on any one of those functions. Someone had previously said from memory, "the queue is definitely over by `getModule`"; after the review, this should be revised to: the lookup tools are adjacent to the capture decision, but the import list does not establish which of them installed the wrapper. This correction is narrow, but useful. It brings the subsequent discussion back from guessing about ownership within the file to the actual ordering requirements.

`memoize` should not be overinterpreted either. It indicates that there are computations or query results here that need to be reused, but the existing records provide no direct relationship between it and queue capture. Early notes linked caching and replay because both occurred around startup; that association was not retained as a basis for the decision.

### Counterexample left in the corner of the review page

A counterexample was written down during the review, but no full meeting minutes were produced:

> If the wrapper is swapped in first, and new chunks can subsequently be found, you cannot infer from that that the old queue has been processed.

This short sentence later became the most useful filter. What it rejects is not the processing of new input, but the practice of replacing old input with new input for validation. Tests or reviews of queue capture must at least distinguish between two batches of content: the portion that existed before takeover and the portion that enters via `push` after takeover. If the two batches are merged into a single "module-queryable" result, the temporal boundary disappears again.

Another review note: do not describe "replay" as "forced execution." The presence of the existing queue indicates that it needs to be included in the discovery path; it does not automatically authorize using the same execution strategy for every chunk. Earlier wording used the term "replay," but someone later interpreted it to mean immediately running all historical content. To be explicit, this is corrected here: this decision concerns handing existing queue content back to the same processing path, not setting forced-execution semantics for all modules.

### Approaches tried but not retained

Two shorter implementation directions were seriously considered; neither became the decision.

**Embed capture in the first query.** The idea was to reuse the existing module-query entry point: when a `getByKeys` or `getByStrings` occurs, process the current queue first, then continue the query. On the surface, this reduces standalone startup logic, but it turns the first query into an implicit switch. Different invocations Fang Ke can trigger it under different conditions, and a delayed query might not happen at all. The capture point therefore ceases to be a stable part of renderer bootstrap and instead becomes an incidental side effect of a query. Rejected.

**Wrap only future `push`.** This direction treated the existing queue as untouchable history and assumed that observing new input after startup was sufficient. It does avoid the ordering issue of processing existing content, but that loses the very goal of this compatibility effort: old and new queues would fall under two different visibility rules. Rejected.

**Connect queue processing and the lazy listener in one step.** This direction was later split apart rather than simply rejected. Whether pending lazy listeners need to be woken is an adjacent startup issue; it has its own timing and batching problems. If this decision treated it as a follow-up action after capture succeeded, the failure symptoms of the two issues would be conflated: it would be impossible to distinguish whether old chunks failed to enter the discovery path or listeners failed to wake at the appropriate time. That part is handed over to the DOC-12 proposal for maintenance; this page retains only the interface boundary.

None of these three is merely another way of saying "not finished." They are directions that were compared: the first makes startup depend on query calls, the second abandons existing input, and the third hard-wires two different timing issues together. The current decision avoids them.

### Legacy operation section, deprecated but still useful for reference

The following is the old troubleshooting sequence, with the original intent preserved:

1. First find any module query.
2. If the query returns an object, consider the queue wrapper to have taken effect.
3. Then check whether modules can be retrieved from subsequent `push`.

These three steps have been deprecated. The criterion in the second step is too strong, treating one successful query as proof that the old queue has been captured. The third step can only indicate that subsequent input may be working normally, and cannot account for where the pre-takeover contents went.

The old paragraph still explains why the assessment was wrong at the time: when both the query and new `push` occurred relatively late, the system's behavior was enough to make people overlook the queue from before startup. The current review no longer follows this sequence. First determine whether the queue already contained anything before the takeover point, then separately observe whether the existing contents and subsequent `push` enter the same discovery path; query results serve only as a signal of subsequent visibility, not as proof that capture is complete.

### Redrawing the scope boundaries

This decision does not define a general-purpose webpack discovery strategy. It also does not define the declaration structures of all Discord modules. The `discord/modules` type surface and `@webpack` query tool in the file provide related clues for troubleshooting, but the current scope covers only the following objects: the existing Discord chunk queue, the post-replacement `push`, the processing path for existing contents, and module discovery that depends on those contents.

Therefore, none of the following claims should be inferred from this page:

- The existence of a `Dispatcher` type means that the related modules are already available after replay.
- A successful `getBySource` query means that the queue takeover occurred at the right time.
- Observing a new `push` means that the old queue has already been processed.
- A lazy listener being awakened means that the capture logic has no boundary issues.

These are not an extra list of negations, but leaps in reasoning that actually occurred in several discussions. Keeping them lets later readers of `discordmodules.ts` know which adjacent concepts cannot serve as evidence for one another.

### Correction for 2025-07

The latest field feedback corrected an earlier statement. Earlier records had treated "retaining a reference to the existing queue" as roughly equivalent to "deferring the processing of all existing modules". This conflates data retention, the replay path and module execution into a single layer, and also leads to unnecessary questions during troubleshooting about whether every chunk was run immediately.

The corrected wording is: first confirm that existing content has not been cut off by replacing `push`, then confirm that both it and subsequent input can enter the applicable discovery paths. "Applicable" preserves the necessary flexibility here: different objects may be consumed under different query conditions, but capture itself cannot cover only future input.

This correction also explains why the presence of `memoize` cannot substitute for observing queue state. Caching may stabilize the result of a particular query, but it cannot establish whether that result comes from content before takeover, content after takeover, or neither. The temporal order must still be established by queue processing itself.

### Current decision

The current decision retains the earlier core tradeoff while tightening its meaning: the installation logic must have an opportunity to process the existing Discord chunk queue before replacing `push`; subsequent input continues to enter through the replaced entry point; module queries only consume discovery results and are not responsible for deciding whether to start capturing. Deferred listeners are not an implicit side effect of this decision.

webpackRequire captures the existing Discord chunk queue before replacing push and replays queued modules.

This requirement is placed here because it brings three points that were repeatedly confused earlier into a single verifiable sequence: the existing queue is captured first, `push` is replaced only afterward, and existing modules return to the processing path through replay. It does not require turning every module query into a synchronous startup barrier, nor does it expand replay to mean forcibly executing arbitrary code.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ExistingQueue
    ExistingQueue --> Captured
    Captured --> PushReplaced
    PushReplaced --> ReplayedModules
    ReplayedModules --> [*]
```

The focus of verification following the decision changes accordingly. Rather than first asking "can a particular module be found", first ask whether a queue already existed when takeover occurred; if so, whether the existing content reached replay; then check whether `push`, after replacement, still feeds into the same discovery side. Only when these three checks are kept distinct can query success or failure be interpreted.

### Related issues, not yet decided here

The wake-up conditions for deferred listeners still need to be handled separately. Deferred listeners and queue capture intersect during startup, but one concerns when existing modules can be discovered, while the other concerns when a pending lookup should continue. Conflating the two would obscure differences in batching, requests in the same round, and error propagation. Discussion of the listener approach can continue in DOC-12; its final timing is not assumed here.

There is also a localized gap: the existing material does not list all callers that depend on the old queue, nor does it provide a complete chain from enqueuing to querying for a specific object. Do not fill in an imagined call graph using type names or function names. The next review should follow `webpackRequire` to find the actual usage sites and confirm which entry point it was interacting with and what the result was at the time; this will fill in the call relationships, but will not change the scope of this decision.

### Archived excerpts

**Early guidance:** "First remember the queue seen before takeover. " This statement still applies, but it must be read together with "do not equate saving with immediate execution".

**Review feedback:** The query tool is an entry point for inspecting modules, not a reason to install a queue wrapper.

**Review reminder:** Subsequent `push` behaving normally does not prove that historical content was normal.

**Current approach:** Capture, replacement and replay are bound together in that order; waking the lazy listener will be discussed separately.

### Appendix: Two retained old examples

**Old example A: Inferring the entire startup state from a single successful query.**

Someone once marked queue capture as "covered" after a module query returned results. This example was later marked as outdated, because it did not distinguish when the content that produced the results had entered the queue. It is still worth retaining: if the review record only says "query succeeded", readers can easily fall into the same inference again.

**Old example B: Placing the `push` wrapper next to the earliest query call.**

This example came from discussions at the time aimed at minimizing changes. It was not syntactically infeasible, but inappropriate in terms of responsibilities: startup capture was tied to incidental caller behavior. It was later decided to separate queue takeover from query side effects. The old example is no longer an implementation recommendation, but it can illustrate why "one fewer segment of the startup path" is not the priority here.

No further queue proposals are provided outside the appendix. The current requirement is to preserve the ordering semantics of the existing decision, and add observations from that entry point after reviewing the actual caller.

versions.body:
# Lazy Lookup Listener Wake-Up Plan

After the first review, the discussion was narrowed back to `src/betterdiscord/webpack/lazy.ts`. Describing the problem as "run it again when the lookup misses" was not precise enough: what needs to be retained is the lookup that has not yet met its conditions, rather than replaying the entire lookup process repeatedly. Repeated queries leave each call site to set its own cadence and revisit modules that have already been seen.

## What Remains from the Original Proposal

Register a pending entry on a miss and check pending entries when a module arrives; that direction remains. Each pending entry must carry at least the original filter criteria and the action to take after completion. A module arriving does not mean that every pending entry can complete; only entries whose conditions match can be removed from the pending set. Non-matching entries remain until the next module arrives.

Remove the original proposal's wording, "run the full filter first, then clear a batch of pending entries at once." It conflates two questions: whether a module matches and whether a given pending entry has been handled safely. A pending entry cannot be removed early merely because another condition in the same batch did not pass.

## Adjacent Code Seen During Review

`lazy.ts` directly introduces the `Webpack` type, `getModule`, `lazyListeners`, and `webpackRequire`, along with `shouldSkipModule`, `getDefaultKey`, `wrapFilter`, and `makeException`. This group of names is enough to show that the change cannot be considered by looking at only one pending array: ordinary lookup, module loading, and filter helper logic are all nearby. The proposal does not require rewriting these entry points; the focus is adding checks at module arrival for the wait state that already exists.

The filtering details are not redefined here. `shouldSkipModule`, default-key selection, and wrapped filtering should retain their respective purposes. If a declarative filter fails during a check, that does not mean all requests awaiting wake-up are invalid; that part remains covered by the investigation record DOC-13.

## Two Implementation Trade-Offs

One option is to schedule the next query immediately after each failed lookup. It is easy to integrate, but wait times and query counts are determined by when calls are made; during startup in particular, it is hard to see which requests are still active.

Another is to put the wait conditions in a listener set and check them only when a module loads. It requires clear registration and removal timing, but keeps the check frequency tied to actual module additions and lets unmatched requests retain their original conditions. The current plan chooses the latter.

It has not yet been decided whether identical conditions should be coalesced. Coalescing can reduce duplicate checks, but it would change how each caller receives its completion signal; until caller dependencies are confirmed, it is not a goal for this iteration.

## Trial Boundaries

Initially, cover only pending entries registered by lazy lookup; do not change the immediate invocations of ordinary `getModule` into listener-based invocations. The rollback is likewise simple: if a wake-up after registration changes an existing lookup result or makes callback ordering impossible to explain, remove the newly added on-arrival check and restore the path in which a miss is handled by the call site. Whether the pending set itself already has other uses still needs to be confirmed at the actual reference sites.

# Lazy Lookup Listener Wake-Up Proposal

This change addresses only the lookups left waiting during startup and discovery. It does not attempt to replace all of webpack's lookup entry points or make module load order a new public constraint. When a caller cannot yet get a module through a lazy lookup, the lookup needs a state that can advance; when the module appears later, that state should advance instead of each caller having to schedule another lookup.

The early draft treated pending entries as a batch of queries that could all be rerun together. This left an undesirable coupling: filtering after a module arrives, completing an individual pending entry, and cleaning up the entire batch of listener entries were all bundled into one step. It looked convenient, but did not specify what to retain when a single condition did not match, a single callback failed, or the same condition was registered more than once.

A later review kept the "register, then wait for a module" approach but dropped the decision to "clear everything at once." The pending set is not a result cache; each entry represents an unfinished lazy lookup. When a module arrives, the handler should only check that module against each entry's condition. Matching entries are processed and removed; nonmatching entries keep waiting. If processing one entry fails, the other entries still get their own chances to proceed later.

`src/betterdiscord/webpack/lazy.ts` is the starting point for this investigation. The file's direct neighbors include `getModule`, `lazyListeners`, and `webpackRequire`; it also imports `shouldSkipModule`, `getDefaultKey`, `wrapFilter`, and `makeException`. These objects do not need their responsibilities redefined in this proposal, but they show that a wake-up point cannot be established with a new array alone: immediate lookup, module retrieval, and filtering helpers all meet along the same path.

## Proposed Scheduling Approach

When a pending entry is registered, retain its original matching condition and completion action. Do not create a second module index. When a module becomes available for lookup, check the entries still in the set in turn:

1. If the condition does not match, leave the entry unchanged;
2. If the condition matches, invoke that entry's completion action;
3. After the completion action completes normally, remove that entry;
4. If the completion action does not complete normally, do not also clean up other entries in the same batch.

This sequence deliberately leaves the business-level ordering of callbacks unspecified. Repeated registrations will also be treated as multiple pending entries for now. Merging identical conditions up front would save a few checks, but it would make two otherwise independent callers share a single completion point; there is not enough reason at present to make that the default behavior.

The old draft suggested running all filters before wake-up, then deciding whether to clear the listener set. That suggestion has been dropped. Filtering results are used only to determine whether the module being processed can satisfy the pending entry being checked; they cannot be used as grounds for batch cleanup. Exception handling for declaration filtering is not being expanded here either: DOC-13 continue to document where to start investigating these failures, so this scheduling change does not decide the exception propagation rules for that area.

## Current Requirements

lazyListeners wake pending lazy lookups when a matching module arrives instead of polling forever.

This sentence defines when wake-up happens, not a promise about module contents. Matching is still determined by the existing lookup conditions; when there is no matching module, the entry stays pending rather than being forced to finish by the arrival of an unrelated module. Ordinary immediate lookups can still return through their existing path; this scheduling applies only to lazy lookups that have already entered a pending state.

## Approaches Not Chosen

Continuous polling has the advantage of not having to maintain a listener set, but it distributes the cost of waiting across individual requests and cannot directly map an actual module arrival to the requests it advances. Failing immediately on a miss is simpler, but requires each caller to add its own retries, leaving different entry points to decide independently when to wait during startup.

Another approach is to rerun the full `getModule` lookup after a module arrives. This would reduce the number of new branches, but would not distinguish between "checking the module at hand for a particular pending condition" and "rescanning existing modules." This proposal does not adopt it; a module's arrival is an opportunity to check pending conditions, not a signal to rebuild all queries.

## Rollback Conditions and Open Questions

If, after integration, unrelated modules cause pending entries to be removed prematurely, the same module causes callbacks to complete more than once, or a callback failure blocks the remaining pending entries, first revert the arrival-triggered wake-up branch. Do not retain half-finished batch cleanup logic. After rollback, misses should again be handled through the original lookup entry point.

Two things remain to be confirmed: whether identical conditions need to be merged in actual usage, and whether the edge-case ordering where a module has already arrived but the listener has only just been registered should be handled by immediate lookup or the registration logic. The former affects callback independence; the latter affects the result of the first registration. Neither should be addressed by expanding the scope of declaration filtering.

# Troubleshooting declaration filtering issues

The initial note recorded just one starting point: if the issue title contains `contain declaration filter failures`, look at `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts` first. The direct dependencies at the top of the file are:

```ts
import type {Webpack} from "discord";
import {webpackRequire} from "./require";
```

## Investigation order at the time

1. First, confirm whether the report actually shows a declaration filtering failure, rather than an ordinary lazy lookup returning no results.
2. Next, look up the call name `wrapDeclarationFilter` and review the call site alongside the result the user saw.
3. If the call site can only be traced to `filter.ts`, note it down first; don't treat the file location as the final determination of ownership.
4. If logs or screenshots from before and after the failure are available, preserve their original content; if all you have is the four-character message "filtering failed," don't yet decide whether it was a declaration mismatch or an error thrown during filtering.

The working hypothesis at the time was that these issues came from webpack declaration filtering criteria becoming narrower. There were no counterexamples yet, and the actual calling pattern had not been confirmed. If a review only turns up a path, stop the investigation at "call and result still needed."

# Troubleshooting declaration filtering issues

This page originally contained only a path and a hastily written assessment. The branches from that review are now included here, with the old assessment left in place.

## First, look at what the report says

If the report only says "declaration filter failure," don't change `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts` yet. The same wording could refer to an empty result seen by the caller, or to the filtering callback failing to return a normal result during execution. Compare the call name, input object, and output seen by the user in one place.

At the top of the file, we can currently see:

```ts
import type {Webpack} from "discord";
import {webpackRequire} from "./require";
```

This shows that it uses types from `Webpack` and the runtime entry point from `./require`; these two lines alone don't establish which layer produced the report.

## Review branches

- If you have the call site for `wrapDeclarationFilter`, but no output: trace through the caller to find the input, then record the object counts before and after filtering. If the counts aren't recorded, stop here.
- If you have output, but it contains no matches: keep the original declaration and filter criteria, and first check whether the declaration's shape has changed.
- If you have exception text or a stack trace: first triage by where the exception occurred; don't relabel it as "no match."
- If you only have a screenshot: keep the exact wording and time shown in it; don't reconstruct the call arguments from memory.

That review still couldn't confirm how it was actually being called. The old notes' approach of "once you see a path, start by making the fix in `filter.ts`" is retained here for reference: without evidence about the call, it can easily mistake the entry file for the fault location; it was later dropped from the actions to take before the stopping point.

# Troubleshooting Declaration Filter Exceptions

This page did not grow out of a complete incident report. The earliest record was a path. Later, someone mixed together filter criteria, lazy lookup, and the file entry point, and only later were "exceptions" separated from "no match". The old paragraphs remain because someone on call still used them to investigate once.

## 2023-03: First Find the File by the Issue Name

The initial note was brief: when you see `contain declaration filter failures`, first look for `filter` in the webpack-related directories. The public technical term was `wrapDeclarationFilter`, so `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts` was treated as the first place to look at the time.

The two lines copied from the file header were:

```ts
import type {Webpack} from "discord";
import {webpackRequire} from "./require";
```

The assessment at the time was "the declaration changed, so the filter may have become narrower". This was only a working hypothesis. That version of the notes had no call site, input declaration, or user output, and did not explain whether the failure occurred before or during matching. When all you have is a path, stop there; do not fill in a seemingly complete explanation of the cause.

### Investigation Side Notes

- When a report says "declaration filter failure", first copy the original wording.
- If it also mentions lazy lookup, record that separately; do not merge the two into one failure just because both terms appear in the same report.
- `filter.ts` is a file entry point that can be traced back to, not a conclusion about responsibility inferred from the filename.

These side notes were reused many times afterward, but there was not enough evidence to support the initial working hypothesis. The original record of that assessment is still preserved here.

## 2023-12: A Review Did Not Separate Empty Results from Exceptions

During the review, the first step was to find `wrapDeclarationFilter`, then return to the file header to confirm its adjacency to `webpackRequire`. This only clarified that "the input should be traced through the caller"; it did not provide a call example that could apply to every report.

The branches recorded at the time were:

```text
A declaration filter failure occurs
├─ Only "not found" or an empty result
│  └─ Save the original declaration, filter criteria, and objects before and after filtering, and compare declaration shapes
├─ Exception text or a stack trace is available
│  └─ Save the original exception text and continue tracing the caller from where it occurred
└─ Only a screenshot or a secondhand account is available
   └─ Do not guess parameters; first obtain the call name, the original text in the screenshot, and the result the user saw
```

This review did not prove that empty results necessarily came from declaration changes. Nor did it prove that the exception text necessarily came from `filter.ts`. If the only input is the issue name, the stopping condition is still the absence of a call and a result.

### Old On-Call Entry (No Longer Applicable Later)

> After finding `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts`, first check the filter criteria in this file; if the criteria look narrower than in the old version, start making changes here.

This passage was not deleted. It turned an "entry point for verification" into a "location to modify", and treated an impression of the old version as a current difference. A later review changed the approach to first saving the call site and original result, then deciding whether implementation changes were needed. The old entry only explains why the investigation continued along the filename at the time; it is not the current stopping rule.

## Review Addendum: Paths Can Guide Navigation, but Cannot Replace Call Evidence

The review comments focused on one issue: the file header can show what this file uses, but cannot show which call branch a report came from. `import type {Webpack} from "discord";` is a type dependency, and `import {webpackRequire} from "./require";` is a runtime adjacency; neither is the user-observed behavior itself.

Therefore, when both an issue name and a call name appear, the record must contain at least three pieces of original evidence:

1. The call name or call site;
2. The declaration or object before it enters filtering;
3. The result the user actually saw, or the original exception text.

Without the first piece, the file can only be used for navigation. Without the second, declaration shapes cannot be compared. Without the third, it is not possible to determine whether there was no match, an exception, or a result that the caller subsequently discarded. Here, "not possible to determine" describes a gap in the evidence at hand, not a direction to switch the investigation to another unified entry point.

## 2024-02: Misreading After Bringing lazy lookup into the Picture

A meeting side note put "declaration filter failure" and "lazy lookup did not get a result in time" on the same line. Later readers could easily follow that wording and treat request timing as part of the filtering semantics. The material on this page has not confirmed that line of reasoning.

On reexamining the path, only local adjacency could still be confirmed: `filter.ts` depends on the `discord` type `Webpack`, and uses `./require`'s `webpackRequire`. This file header does not establish the wake-up order of the lazy listener, nor does the name `wrapDeclarationFilter` establish the input format for every caller.

If a report also includes lazy lookup:

- First separate "what the filter result is" and "when the result becomes visible" into two lines;
- When the filter result is empty, save the declaration and filter criteria;
- When the result arrives late, save the chronological order of calls and the UI state the user saw;
- Combine the two back into one record only when they line up at the same call site, with the same batch of inputs and the same result.

If there is only one screenshot, do not directly interpret the delay shown in it as rejection by the filter. The screenshot can serve as an original result artifact, but the call and input are still missing.

### Meeting Excerpt, Original Meaning Preserved

> Do not treat `filter.ts` as the fix location yet. Separate "no match" from "threw", then look at who calls it.

This addendum changed the investigation order, but did not provide a new implementation conclusion. It also did not resolve the questions on the lazy lookup side; related issues remain at the end of the page.

## 2024-09: Record of an Unsuccessful Attempt

There was an attempt to trace backward by filename: starting from `filter.ts`, the investigation traced upward for related calls, then classified the report as a "declaration mismatch" upon seeing the call name. That assessment does not hold up without the original output. A later review did not find enough material to prove that the report really was a declaration mismatch, so it cannot be recorded as a reproduced result.

The failure was not finding the wrong path, but collapsing three different levels into one:

- File entry point: `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts`;
- Public search term: `wrapDeclarationFilter`;
- Observed behavior: the result or exception the user saw.

Record these three levels separately during investigation. If the file entry point is missing, the public search term can be used for navigation; if the public search term is missing, do not freely guess the call based on "declaration filtering"; if the observed behavior is missing, do not substitute a function name for the result.

### Stopping Conditions for the Unsuccessful Attempt

If only `filter.ts` is found, stop at the path record.

If `wrapDeclarationFilter` is found but the input cannot be found, stop at the call record.

If the input is found but there is no user result, stop at the input record.

If the exception exists only in a secondhand account, preserve that account and mark it as unverified; do not format it as a stack trace.

These stopping conditions are more restrictive than "keep tracing upward", but they prevent a navigation step from being misrepresented as a complete retrospective.

## 2025-01: Addendum on Responsibility Boundaries

What this page can directly address is local investigation near this file entry point in BetterDiscord Desktop Runtime. Integration with adjacent packages, the Electron compatibility directory, and joint debugging with callers are not covered by the material on this page. If a call falls outside these boundaries, preserve the path and the original issue wording, then hand it over to the appropriate maintainer; do not fill in implementation relationships on their behalf.

The objects that can be verified locally are:

| Object | What Can Be Done | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| `src/betterdiscord/webpack/filter.ts` | Read local declarations and direct dependencies | Not enough to establish the report's source |
| `wrapDeclarationFilter` | Use as a search entry point to trace calls | Not a substitute for inputs and outputs |
| `Webpack` | Identify type adjacency in the file header | Not enough to explain runtime results |
| `webpackRequire` | Identify runtime adjacency in the file header | Not enough to prove the specific call sequence |

Adjacent projects are not listed here as confirmed owners. When the corresponding artifact cannot be obtained, responsibility boundaries remain handoff questions only: where the call comes from, who can provide the original input, and who can confirm the user result must still be answered based on the actual call.

## 2025-05: Current Verification Guidance Near the End of the Page

Start by tracing back from the behavior the user saw, rather than making changes directly based on the filename. If the behavior is "the declaration did not match", save the declaration, filter criteria, and returned result; if the behavior is an exception, save the original exception text and where it occurred. These two types of records may point to the same function, but they are not interchangeable.

The current implementation semantics are preserved here as a directly quotable statement: **wrapDeclarationFilter contains a throwing declaration filter and treats that exception as a non-match.**

This statement appears only in the current verification section. It explains why an exception may ultimately appear as no match, but does not establish that any specific report necessarily followed this path. Specific reports must still be routed using the tree below.

```text
A user reports declaration filter failure
├─ The original exception text can be obtained
│  ├─ The exception occurred within the declaration filtering call
│  │  └─ Check the result under the semantics of "treat the exception as a non-match", then preserve the original exception
│  └─ The exception location is outside the call
│     └─ Do not attribute it to declaration filtering; follow the actual stack trace to the level above
├─ There is no exception, and the result is empty or missing
│  ├─ The declaration before filtering and the filter criteria are available
│  │  └─ Compare the declaration shape, criteria, and returned result
│  └─ The input or criteria are missing
│     └─ Stop at the call record and request the original evidence from the reporter
└─ Only an issue name, screenshot, or secondhand account is available
   └─ Preserve the original wording, and first find the actual call to `wrapDeclarationFilter` and the user result
```

### Actions Within the Branches

**A. The original exception text is available.**

Save the exception text first; do not start by rewriting it as "filter failure". Confirm whether the exception occurred within the declaration filtering call or in the level above that called it. If the location can be mapped to the call itself, then check whether the final result was treated as a non-match; preserve the exception as well, because "non-match" is the externally visible behavior, not a substitute for the original exception text.

If the stack trace contains only file paths and no call relationships, the paths can only help with tracing. Do not infer from the location of `filter.ts` that there is a `Webpack` type incompatibility, and do not infer from the presence of `webpackRequire` that it threw the exception.

**B. There is no exception, but the result is empty.**

Save the declaration before filtering, the criteria, and the result side by side. First compare whether the actual declaration changed, then check whether the filter criteria excluded it. Without the object before filtering, an empty result cannot be used to infer a declaration change. If all you have is the empty UI the user saw, record only that UI behavior; do not directly describe it as the function returning an empty result.

**C. The result arrives late or looks like lazy lookup.**

Create a separate timing record: the order in which calls occurred, the order in which results appeared, and what the user saw in between. Continue examining the relationship between filtering and lazy lookup only when all three can be tied to the same call. Without timing information, stop at the observed-behavior level; do not merge "late arrival" into "non-match".

**D. Only a screenshot or a secondhand account is available.**

Preserve the text and UI state in the screenshot as they are. First obtain the call site for `wrapDeclarationFilter`, then obtain the input and result. Do not use a familiar function name to fill in parameters that the screenshot does not show, and do not turn "someone said it threw an error" into an exception record.

## Stopping Points and Handoffs for the Current Page

If any of the following is missing, stop the investigation at the lowest level for which evidence has been obtained; do not continue piecing together a conclusion:

- No actual call site: do not treat a path as a call;
- No declaration before filtering: do not treat an empty result as a declaration change;
- No filter criteria: do not judge which object was excluded;
- No user result or original exception text: do not fill in externally visible behavior locally;
- The stack trace points to an adjacent project: retain the questions for handoff, and do not write up the adjacent implementation on its behalf.

Put the path, call name, and original observed behavior obtained so far into the same record. If only one of them can be obtained, state explicitly which ones are missing. `BDR-203` later requested the actual way the call was made and the result the user saw, but those two specific pieces of evidence had still not been included when the current version of this page was created; this page therefore does not pretend that the review has been completed.

## Related Issues Not Yet Split Out

The request timing of lazy lookup and the result timing of declaration filtering may still appear in the same report. This page does not have enough evidence to determine whether the same caller connects them. Another unresolved point is whether the caller still leaves a visible exception record when an exception is presented as no match; that depends on the actual call and logs, not on the file header.

If an actual call is obtained later, prioritize placing it under the corresponding branch, together with the input and user result. Do not merely append a "confirmed" conclusion; it must be clear which original stopping condition has been lifted.

## Appendix: Old Meeting Guidance (Retained)

> When you see `filter.ts`, start with the filter criteria, and look for the call only if the declaration appears unchanged.

This guidance remains in the appendix because it explains why the early notes repeatedly started from the file entry point. It has been superseded by the current order above: first establish the observed behavior and the call, then compare declarations. Especially when only the issue name is available, the old guidance can mistake "no evidence" for "the declaration has not changed".

The appendix's "look at the criteria first" can be a local step when reading a file, but cannot serve as incident attribution or a stopping point for modifications.

versions.body:
# Plugin Metadata and Recovery Decisions

This page originally put plugin metadata and recovery issues on the same page because both arose during the same compatibility wrap-up effort. This grouping was not so wrong that it needed to be deleted, but it left an overly convenient assumption in place: seeing local files, requests, and logs around addonstore.ts led to treating recovery as an action that could end at a single point.

During later review, this assumption was not developed further. It was retained because many old troubleshooting entry points still lead here; removing it would leave later readers unable to see why anyone had once treated metadata reporting and recovery closure as the same thing.

## The Original Breakdown

The file entry point identified at the time was `src/betterdiscord/modules/addonstore.ts`. The top of the file directly imported:

```ts
import path from "path";
import fs from "fs";
import request from "@polyfill/request";
import Logger from "@common/logger";
```

These four dependencies were once used to make a very rough judgment: once metadata needs to organize local information, request results, and diagnostic information, the report should not directly reuse all the fields of internal objects. This judgment led to the first decision: reports should retain only the results actually visible to the caller, record success and failure separately, and not treat `filename`, `path`, or `private` as default output.

Here, "record separately" does not mean combining the two types of calls into a polished status summary. A successful result may be enough to confirm that metadata can be read; a failed result should preserve the failure itself rather than disguise it as success with an empty object. No fixed field list was provided at the time, nor was it confirmed that all callers followed the same path. The scope is narrow: it only requires that reporting not casually expose or concatenate internal location information.

Recovery issues were placed alongside this because a failure report could easily be misread as meaning that recovery had ended. The old draft used a provisional criterion: as long as the entry point was available again, recovery could be considered closed. This criterion is now retained as a historical position and can no longer be applied directly. It conflated "can enter again" with "all subsequent recovery surfaces have been exited", and it was not mapped to an actual workflow or fallback entry point.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

| Approach | Benefit at the time | Reason for rejection or retention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treat metadata reporting and recovery closure as one task | Short records, with only one troubleshooting entry point | A success report cannot prove that recovery steps have ended; a failure report cannot indicate where recovery should resume either |
| Select fields directly from internal objects for reporting | Implementation appeared straightforward | The names `filename`, `path`, and `private` themselves remind us that internal location information and externally visible results do not share the same boundary |
| Define a complete set of public fields up front | Makes comparison easier for callers | There were not enough call samples at the time, so a field list would turn an unverified structure into a commitment |
| Keep reporting and recovery as two separate records | Requires capturing one additional set of information from the investigation | Allows report results and the location of recovery execution to be checked separately; ultimately adopted |

What was adopted was not a conclusion that "metadata is now safe" or "recovery is now closed", but a recording sequence. First confirm what the report retained, then find the steps recovery actually went through; only after both sides can be explained clearly should we discuss whether the word "closure" can be used.

This also explains why the old draft did not present `path`, `fs`, requests, and logs as a causal chain. They are merely the immediately adjacent elements visible in addonstore.ts. The presence of requests in a file does not mean those requests are recovery actions; the presence of logs does not mean those logs cover every failure branch. Treating these adjacent elements too much like a central hub early on is why this page later needed an addendum.

## Counterexamples from Later Reviews

The supplementary material is in BDR-206 and BDR-207. The former requires separately retaining the visible results of "report addon metadata safely" from one successful call and one failed call, and a counterexample has already been added; the accompanying notes still explicitly identify one unconfirmed point. This counterexample is enough to refute the idea that "as long as the successful sample looks normal, the reporting boundary is already stable".

The counterexample did not prove which field should be made public, nor did it prove that the failure necessarily came from addonstore.ts. It only forces the recording method back to a narrower claim: success and failure cannot substitute for one another. If only the successful call is saved, readers cannot determine whether information that should not have appeared was exposed during failure; if only the failed call is saved, they also cannot determine whether the normal path can still provide the necessary results.

BDR-207 leave a different kind of gap: the build logs need to be traced to find the steps that actually execute "close every recovery surface", and the responsible workflow and fallback entry point need to be filled in. This page has not presented that to-do as an accomplished fact. It changes only the earlier decision: whether recovery has reached closure can no longer be judged by whether the entry point is available again; at a minimum, it must be possible to identify the execution steps and where to return in case of failure.

Accordingly, "it can end once the entry point is available again" in the old draft is marked as outdated. It was useful in early troubleshooting because it prevented metadata issues from expanding indefinitely into generalized failures; but it is no longer sufficient to describe recovery completion. The judgment represented by the original sentence is retained so that, when old links land on this page, it is still possible to explain why further tracing stopped at the time.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> RecordReportResults
    RecordReportResults --> SuccessfulSample
    RecordReportResults --> FailedSample
    SuccessfulSample --> FindRecoverySteps
    FailedSample --> FindRecoverySteps
    FindRecoverySteps --> workflowLocated
    FindRecoverySteps --> Unconfirmed
    workflowLocated --> CheckFallbackEntryPoint
    CheckFallbackEntryPoint --> CanDiscussClosure
```

"Can discuss closure" in the diagram is deliberately not a completed state. It means that report records and recovery tracing come back together here, not that every metadata call triggers recovery or that every recovery branch returns to addonstore.ts.

## Decisions Retained

1. For metadata reporting, retain the respective visible results of the successful call and the failed call. The two results must be readable together, but they are not required to have the same fields.
2. `filename`, `path`, and `private` may be used only as location clues for internal review, and must not be included in the output by default just because "metadata needs to be reported".
3. addonstore.ts is one of the entry points for this round of verification. It can help review the adjacency among local information, requests, and logs, but this is not grounds for concluding that it owns the entire recovery process.
4. "close every recovery surface" can be recorded as complete only after the actual workflow has been located and the fallback entry point has also been filled in. The existing records still lack the execution location for this part.

The second item is the only boundary truly finalized on this page. It is not a field specification for all plugin objects, nor does it replace callers' own compatibility agreements. The reason for adopting this boundary is specific: the issue at the time was reporting metadata, not copying internal objects to the outside; including paths and private information would not help distinguish success from failure, and would also make later troubleshooting depend on incidental internal structure.

The first and fourth items concern the sequence of recording and judgment. The former prevents a successful sample from being treated as all the evidence, while the latter prevents re-entry from being treated as recovery completion. Both arose from the practical work in this round of wrap-up and should not be interpreted as a general model of the addon lifecycle.

## Old Entry Points That Still Lead Here

Old troubleshooting records point to this file using terms such as addon, public, filename, path, and private. These entry points are still useful for revisiting the discussion at the time: they explain why the reporting boundary received attention first. But they are not enough to answer who performs recovery, or to establish any single log entry as definitive proof.

If the recovery section needs to be filled in, first follow BDR-207 to find the execution steps and fallback entry point in the build logs; if the reporting boundary needs to be reviewed, revisit the visible results retained from the two calls, one successful and one failed, in BDR-206. DOC-17 cover a separate piece of compatibility work on theme identifiers and should not be used to fill these two gaps.

This decision record was not subsequently rewritten as a comprehensive lifecycle description. The old judgment remains, as do its reasons; the genuinely missing workflow and fallback locations should remain identified as missing, rather than being replaced by filenames, imports, or a single successful call.

# Renderer Readiness and Build Metadata Migration

This page has long been used as the migration guide for the 2026.09 compatibility train, but at first it was only a record tracing an old issue name to a module file. The old version did not distinguish among the states "the waiting condition has been met," "build information exists," and "build information has been restored to where it is used later," nor did it leave behind the actual callers. The classification remains here because someone later may return from the same terms to the same entry point.

## Navigating the old entry point

The early records gave the following first stop:

```text
Issue name or call name
        |
```
