```text
src/betterdiscord/modules/editor.ts
        |
        +-- Logger
        +-- DOMManager
        +-- getAllModules / webpackRequire
        +-- Patcher
```

At the time, this diagram was treated as a simplified diagram of the startup discovery chain. That description now seems too broad, but it explains why the page title, old notes, and several local search habits all point to the editor module: the file header contained direct dependencies related to DOM management, webpack queries, and patching all at once, so when reading code it was easy to see it as the convergence point for all startup issues.

The old migration ticket required first opening `src/betterdiscord/modules/editor.ts`, marking things starting with the imports at the top of the file, and then looking outward along the issue name and call name. It did not require finding a declaration named readiness or build metadata in the file; the old record assumed that adjacent modules were sufficient to establish the relationship. This assumption later caused two inconveniences: when the waiting point and build-information restoration were changed together, it was difficult to know which item changed the behavior; and when tracing back only from imports, the record did not contain enough information to associate a particular caller with a particular startup cycle.

Therefore, the old migration order is retained below, with the later-added checkpoints written in adjacent locations. They are for people who still need to handle the old entry point, not a redefinition of the implementation ownership of editor.ts.

## Steps in the old migration ticket

1. First enter the editor module from the issue name, rather than starting from a guessed webpack module number. The first goal in the old record was to confirm that the file currently being read was the module file, not a build-artifact fragment with the same name.
2. Copy down the direct dependencies at the file header. The record once listed `Logger`, `DOMManager`, `getAllModules`, `webpackRequire`, and `Patcher`. These names were used to pin down the reading position at the time; they are not themselves an indication that client build metadata has been restored.
3. Then find the callers that use `wait for renderer readiness`. The old version treated "finding the string in search results" as a signal that migration could proceed; the later addendum required leaving at least the actual version, entry point, and current result. Without these three items, the caller remains pending.
4. Trigger the job corresponding to `recover client build metadata` separately from the automation entry point, leaving the job, commit, and actual artifact name. The old version only said "restore build information" and did not require these three values, so it was impossible to distinguish one job from another local observation.
5. Only after both records are complete should they be put back into the same round of startup checks. Here, "put back" is only to keep the investigation order continuous; it does not mean that the two items must be implemented by the same module, nor that a waiting result can substitute for the build-information result.

The old version combined the third and fourth steps into the sentence "wait for renderer, then restore metadata." This is exactly the most misleading part of the page. The waiting condition describes when to continue looking; the restoration record describes what must be left behind. Both may appear in one startup issue, but if one item is missing from the record, it should not be replaced by the other.

## What to retain when migrating out of the old record

This type of migration did not provide a source change that could be directly substituted, nor did it freeze a new function entry point. What can be migrated is mainly the way of recording things.

- The original issue names and call names can still serve as search starting points. They explain the old entry point, but are insufficient as a conclusion about the relationship.
- The file path should still be written as `src/betterdiscord/modules/editor.ts`. The path is the location of the old investigation material; in migration notes, do not rewrite it as the implementation location for renderer readiness or metadata.
- Imports at the file header can serve as adjacency clues while reading. `getAllModules` and `webpackRequire` appear in the same place, but that does not mean either call site has obtained client build metadata; `DOMManager` and Patcher likewise cannot substitute for a renderer state record.
- The waiting item must be tied to a caller that is still in use, and include the version, entry point, and current result. The old version did not have these fields; if only the old description is copied after migration, it will still return to the problem of "assuming coverage just by seeing the term."
- The restoration item must be tied to an automation job, and include the job, commit, and actual artifact name. Here, the artifact name is the local record needed to distinguish job results; it is not a request to generate an additional build manifest.

The old materials once suggested that as long as a webpack query existed near the editor module, renderer waiting and metadata restoration could be submitted as a single change. The suggestion is retained below for identifying it during historical lookup:

> On the editor side, wait first, then supplement the build information from the webpack result; the old entry point can be migrated once the same verification has passed.

This suggestion is no longer suitable as a migration criterion. It did not distinguish the validation targets or require confirmation of the caller. It is retained not because it is reliable, but because it explains why early records did not separate the two types of results.

## Restoring the old path

The restoration described on this page concerns only the investigation entry point and migration records; it does not describe a runtime rollback. If the new record has not yet been filled in with the actual caller or automation job information, restore the reading entry point to the editor module and resume searches for the old issue name and call name; do not write an unverified module relationship into the old entry.

After restoration, the original two tasks should still be kept separate:

```text
Old entry: editor.ts
    |
    +-- Waiting item: find a caller still in use
    |
    +-- Restoration item: leave job and artifact records from the automation entry point
```

There is no "restored as verified" status here. The old entry provides only a starting position. Restoring it means that the next investigation can still find the same file and the same set of imports; it does not mean that renderer is ready, nor that client build metadata has been successfully restored.

## Later review addendum

During later organization, the waiting item was placed at BDR-209. The local description on the card requires finding a caller that is still using `wait for renderer readiness`, and checking its actual version, entry point, and current result. This filled in the biggest omission in the old migration ticket: not merely knowing that a waiting concept exists, but knowing at which entry it still occurs.

The build-information restoration item was placed at BDR-210. The item requires triggering the corresponding job from an existing automation entry point in the repository, leaving the job, commit, and actual artifact name. The card was later processed once, but the public addendum still states that `recover client build metadata` has one unconfirmed point. The completed status must not be interpreted as meaning that all restoration paths are clear, nor should the unconfirmed point be written as a failed implementation.

BDR-209 subsequently underwent documentation review. The review did not add any new call edges to the old diagram, so this page does not expand the original editor.ts diagram into a complete startup chain. The old diagram only explains the reading order at the time; the card record separates the objects that need continued investigation.

DOC-20 record another set of discovery work in the same compatibility train: minified webpack chunks and cache miss. They can serve as navigation to parallel material, but should not be used to fill the missing readiness caller or metadata job result on this page. The two pages use similar webpack vocabulary but handle different record objects.

## Scope of the corrections to the old wording

This addendum only corrects what on-site information the migration record should retain; it does not rewrite the old page as a description of the current startup architecture. Investigation can still begin from the editor module; the two issues can still be placed in the same round of compatibility investigation; but the file's import list can no longer be treated as evidence that both items have been confirmed.

The old page also leaves one unresolved question: if the same caller involves both renderer readiness and build-information restoration, should the record go under the waiting item, or serve as a note for the restoration job? The existing materials provide no consistent classification. For now, record it under the actual entry that appears first, and no longer use the editor module's location to decide its ownership.

## Archived excerpt

The old version's core judgment was "first investigate from editor, then restore metadata after renderer is ready." It is suitable for reminding readers not to immediately assume that discovery objects are already available at the earliest stage of startup, but it is not suitable for directly guiding migration. The material that can now be genuinely reviewed should include the caller information for a waiting item that is still in use, as well as the job, commit, and artifact name left by the automation job corresponding to the restoration item.

If all you have is the old path and imports, first treat them as historical navigation. If all you have is the to-be-investigated description on the card, also do not assert in reverse that editor.ts is the implementation location. Taken together, the two sides explain why this old migration ticket exists and which parts still need to be filled in by the actual entry point.

# Markdown Wrapper Compatibility Decision

The initial draft kept two phrases side by side solely because they were part of the same round of work to finalize public-call compatibility: adapt the markdown wrapper and bind public data to an addon. After rechecking the entry points, the conclusion to retain is not "they are related", but a narrower statement: they currently need to be investigated by tracing different objects.

The former has a clear local starting point: `src/betterdiscord/ui/base/markdown.tsx`. For the latter, the available excerpts contain no corresponding read/write location. Describing the two tasks as a single complete call chain would conflate filenames, task names, and the actual relationships between objects. The initial draft's decision to keep the two lines of work separate stands, but the reason for separating them needs to be made clear.

---

### Initial Assessment and Its Limits

The earliest working assessment was that public-call compatibility issues might surface in the markdown wrapper layer, so `markdown.tsx` was opened first. This assessment is suitable as a starting point for reading the code, not as a conclusion about the cause.

"Might surface here" encompasses at least three distinct levels:

- The two task descriptions appeared in the same round of compatibility work;
- The markdown wrapper has a source-code entry point that can be opened directly;
- The addon's public data binding is another area of behavior that needs to be verified.

These three levels are not interchangeable. The first explains why they were included in the same decision; the second explains where to start examining wrapper adaptation; the third makes clear that a filename cannot answer the question of data binding.

The initial draft already avoided an easy leap: seeing `markdown.tsx` and then explaining public-data anomalies as a markdown implementation issue. Even after review, there is still not enough material to support that step. A file path can help locate the wrapper layer, but it cannot automatically be extended to paths for writing, saving, or displaying addon data.

Likewise, the opposite conclusion, "the two are unrelated", cannot be drawn. Both belong to the context of public-call and compatibility work, and a specific object may connect the two lines of work in the future. No such object, direction, or reference currently exists, so this decision does not prematurely manufacture a point of intersection.

### What Was Actually Seen in the File This Time

The header of `src/betterdiscord/ui/base/markdown.tsx` provides a set of direct dependencies, not a complete implementation. The currently visible content is as follows:

```ts
import React from "@modules/react";
import DiscordModules from "@modules/discordmodules";
import type {Rules, SimpleMarkdown} from "discord/modules";
import type {ComponentClass, PropsWithChildren} from "react";
```

These lines have two distinct levels. `React` and `DiscordModules` are runtime imports; they show that the file obtains React-related capabilities and an entry point to Discord modules at runtime. `Rules`, `SimpleMarkdown`, `ComponentClass`, and `PropsWithChildren`, on the other hand, are imported as types, indicating that the wrapper file's declarations cover markdown rules and expressions, as well as React component types and the shape of children.

Not every import here should be interpreted as a data-transfer connection. In particular, the presence of `DiscordModules` only confirms that it is a runtime dependency of this file, and its name cannot establish that any of its members is the addon's public data, nor can it establish that this file binds data to the addon.

Type imports should not be treated as background that can be skipped either. The wrapper handles more than just "whether the module can be found", and may also need to accommodate external objects through representable component and rule shapes. At a minimum, `Rules` and `SimpleMarkdown` keep the markdown-side declaration boundaries in the file; `ComponentClass` and `PropsWithChildren` keep the type shapes that component wrapping needs to account for in the same place.

Therefore, a more accurate description of the current path is: it brings React component shapes, module entry points provided by Discord, and markdown-related types together in a local wrapper file. This description is sufficient for someone to continue checking the wrapper's adaptation from here, without overstating the file as a complete rendering path or portraying it as the only place where addon data binding occurs.

### Rejected attribution shortcuts

The first wording rejected during review was "all issues following public calls should first be attributed to the markdown wrapper layer". Its appeal was straightforward: the path name was obvious, and the file header also contained React and Discord module entry points. It could quickly produce a seemingly unified explanation.

The problem is that this apparent unity comes from the filename rather than confirmed object relationships. The existing file header does not show the addon's public data object, does not show a binding operation, and does not show where state is stored or used after a call ends. Filling these gaps directly with responsibilities assigned to the wrapper layer would lead subsequent reviewers to search for nonexistent answers in a file that is already open.

The second approach not adopted was to strip all type imports out of the compatibility assessment and examine only runtime imports. This approach is more cautious than the first, but would reduce wrapper adaptation to "as long as it loads". For a wrapper, whether component categories, the shape of children, markdown rules, and markdown expressions can be described correctly is likewise something that requires further examination of the actual declarations.

Type names alone cannot establish runtime order, nor can they explain the behavior of a specific rule; what they provide is another constraint. If the actual wrapper declarations later turn out not to match these shapes, the issue does not lose its significance for compatibility just because types are not loaded at runtime. Accordingly, this record neither presents types as data flow nor removes them from the wrapper adaptation track.

The third rejected approach was to wait until the complete call relationships were available before recording a decision. This would indeed avoid documenting uncertainty, but it would also erase the process behind why this entry point was chosen initially and why shortcut attribution was rejected. The facts currently available are already sufficient to decide one local matter: wrapper adaptation and data binding cannot be conflated into a single track merely because they appear in the same batch. Once the complete call relationships are available, points of intersection can be added, but waiting for them cannot be a reason not to record this judgment.

### The chosen separation approach

This record uses two independent lines of verification. The first starts from `src/betterdiscord/ui/base/markdown.tsx` and covers the adaptation boundaries of the markdown wrapper; the second centers on bind public data to an addon and covers the state that needs to be confirmed after public data is handed to the addon.

The first line concerns whether the wrapped object can still appear in acceptable component and rule shapes. The existing imports already provide terms to guide further inspection: `Rules`, `SimpleMarkdown`, `ComponentClass`, and `PropsWithChildren`. If these types are later seen participating in input, output, or wrapping relationships at actual declaration or usage sites, those findings should fall under this line; if they are only seen on the declaration surface, retain only the facts established at that level.

The second line concerns the act of binding public data itself and its results. It cannot simply be replaced with "whether markdown nodes appear". Whether the wrapped content is rendered and whether the data has been bound to the addon are two judgments that can independently hold true or fail. The existing fragments do not provide enough evidence to select any particular failure mode, so no outcome is assumed here.

Separating them does not mean reducing the importance of the second item. Precisely because the wrapper file cannot answer the public data binding question, a separate object of investigation and a separate entry point need to be retained. If it is shoehorned into a UI wrapping issue, any state observed later will first be misclassified: the data may not have been bound, it may not have been used as expected after binding, or it may never have passed through this local path at all.

The diagram below shows only the reading branches chosen for this investigation, not that a transfer relationship already exists between the two objects:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> markdown_work
    state "adapt the markdown wrapper" as markdown_work
    markdown_work --> markdown_file
    state "src/betterdiscord/ui/base/markdown.tsx" as markdown_file
    [*] --> addon_work
    state "bind public data to an addon" as addon_work
    addon_work --> addon_state
    state "Confirming the state after binding" as addon_state
```

Both starting edges in the diagram come from the current work object. The first leads to the frozen source code path; the second stops at confirmation of the post-binding state. There is no edge from `markdown_file` to `addon_state`, because the current material does not establish such a relationship.

### Reading boundaries for the wrapper track

When returning to `markdown.tsx`, do not start by assigning this file a complete role in the system. First distinguish between two kinds of dependencies: `@modules/react` and `@modules/discordmodules` are runtime entry points; the four names from `discord/modules` and `react` form the type surface.

This distinction helps avoid misreading the arrangement of import statements as the implementation order. Runtime dependencies indicate which entry points the file will obtain, not the members inside those entry points or the order in which they are called. Type dependencies indicate what shapes the wrapper needs to express in its declarations, not that runtime objects necessarily move under the same names or in the same directions.

Next, look at where the actual wrapper object uses these types. If rule objects are received, transformed, filtered, or returned, the relevant actions are candidate facts about wrapper adaptation; if component shapes are narrowed or extended, that should also fall along the same track. Conversely, the names `Rules` or `SimpleMarkdown` alone cannot establish whether a particular rule has been changed.

`React` also cannot be generalized to mean "all UI issues are here". In this file, it is an explicitly visible runtime dependency; together with `ComponentClass` and `PropsWithChildren`, it makes component wrapping a reasonable direction for review. The specific components, rendering hierarchy, and callers need to be supplied by actual code snippets, not filled in from the current file header.

`DiscordModules` must be handled with the same restraint. It is a module entry point visible in the wrapper file, which is enough to show that markdown wrapping does not depend solely on React's static types; however, no material shows what it currently retrieves, or whether this entry point carries the public data of the addon. If specific members can be confirmed later, their names and usage locations should be added under the wrapper track, rather than backfilled as "known all along".

Ultimately, the question this track needs to answer is not "whether markdown is important", but whether the wrapper's inputs, rule relationships, and component boundaries can still be correctly expressed after the compatibility adjustments. The existing material is not yet sufficient to answer questions about specific implementation details, but it is enough to establish which object to continue examining.

### The data-binding track does not borrow a filename

The subject of bind public data to an addon is the binding relationship between the addon and public data. It and the markdown wrapper are both part of this compatibility work, but appearing in the same batch does not give them the same source code association.

One valid reminder left by the draft is: the state after the call completes needs to be confirmed separately. Here, "state" does not presuppose a page location, field name, or fixed display format. The current material contains none of these details, nor any success or failure samples. Writing an unspecified presentation form as an established fact would only add a false target for subsequent verification.

This line should also not be written as "complete as long as the data exists". There may still be undisplayed object transformations or usage locations between the binding action and the subsequent state; likewise, observing a particular result does not automatically mean that the binding occurs in the markdown file. The current decision only requires these two levels to be recorded separately: one is whether binding occurred, and the other is the state that needs to be confirmed after binding.

Therefore, if later material adds an object, call entry point, or result on the addon side, only the data-binding track needs to be updated; there is no need to bring the markdown file into it for the sake of completeness. The judgment that "the two tracks are not yet connected" needs to be revised only when a new excerpt clearly points to the addon's public data object and explicitly states that it passes through or is constrained by the markdown wrapper.

This is not about raising the update threshold, but about preventing "the same round of work" from being miswritten as "the same implementation boundary". An excerpt that proves only binding should advance only the binding track; an excerpt that proves only a wrapper rule or component shape should advance only the wrapper track. If a shared object exists in the future, the object and the direction it occupies should be written out, rather than using "the two are related" to obscure the specific relationship.

### Assumptions retained in the draft

The draft's working assumptions have not all been withdrawn: the markdown wrapper remains a reasonable starting point for checking compatibility issues. What needs to be withdrawn is the unstated part of the assumption that is easy to read as a conclusion—that because we start from the wrapper, we can prioritize explaining the addon data issue.

The withdrawal is not because an opposing implementation has already been found, but because the imports reviewed do not support this explanation. They support understanding from the wrapper file how React, Discord modules, and markdown types appear alongside one another; they do not support placing the data-binding action in that file.

The old assumption should remain in the document because it explains where the current decision came from. Without it, later readers would see only a very cautious split and would not know why the two things were initially put together. Retaining the old judgment also avoids another form of historical cleanup: rewriting the original entry-point judgment as if a complete call relationship had already been available at the time.

However, when citing this old judgment, it needs to be read together with the correction. It explains "why the markdown file was opened first", not "the data binding already happened here". The difference between these two sentences is precisely the boundary this review needs to preserve.

### Handling of compatibility scope

This decision discusses public calls and compatibility; it does not give the two phrases a system scope larger than the existing material. The markdown wrapper issue is not generalized to all markdown rendering issues; addon data binding is not generalized to all addon lifecycle issues.

This narrowing has two practical effects. First, when reading `markdown.tsx`, the focus can remain on wrapper objects, rule types, and component shape, without bringing in themes, settings, or other runtime surfaces that do not appear. Second, when checking data binding, the focus can return to the addon's public data object and post-call state, rather than first looking for the cause in the wrapper layer merely because the path names are similar.

A common misreading in compatibility work is to treat "having the same public entry point" as "having the same internal point of responsibility". The material available this time supports only the former kind of parallel treatment at the work level, not the latter kind of merging at the implementation level. What has been finalized is how documentation and review are divided, not where some as-yet-unseen final implementation belongs.

If it later turns out that the wrapper only presents data, the documentation should continue to distinguish "presentation" from "binding". If it turns out to participate in converting data objects, the objects between which the conversion occurs need to be specified; if it turns out that the two tracks were merely adjusted together as part of the same release finalization, that result should also be retained as a work arrangement, not passed off as a code relationship.

### Where future additions belong

If new material concerns only markdown rules, wrapper components, or the specific use of `DiscordModules`, it should be added to the wrapper track. New content needs to indicate whether it adds information about the input shape, rule relationships, component boundaries, or module entry point, without also having to rewrite the addon data section.

If new material concerns only the process of handing public data to an addon or the state after binding, it should be added to the data-binding track. It may change the assessment for the second track, but it should not be used to work backward and infer the responsibilities of `markdown.tsx`.

Only a new snippet that meets both conditions is sufficient to change the current division into tracks: it explicitly points to the addon's public data object; it also clearly shows that this object passes through, affects, or is processed by the markdown wrapper. The appearance of `React`, `DiscordModules`, `Rules`, `SimpleMarkdown`, `ComponentClass`, or `PropsWithChildren` alone does not satisfy this condition. These names are terms for locating material to read further, not proof that the two tracks have already intersected.

The areas that have yet to be fleshed out should also remain organized according to this division: what markdown object the wrapper actually receives, where rule types come into play as constraints, how the component shape is passed to callers, which members `DiscordModules` specifically accesses; and which object hands public data to the addon, and where the state should be confirmed after binding is complete. These are not a list of to-dos that can be merged, but facts that each side needs to obtain separately.

### Current decision

The decision is to maintain two independent compatibility verification tracks: use `src/betterdiscord/ui/base/markdown.tsx` as the local entry point for adapt the markdown wrapper, and continue to review components, rule types, and direct module dependencies; retain bind public data to an addon as an independent addon data-binding issue, and confirm the post-binding state separately.

The file header supports the first track's local connections to React, Discord modules, markdown rules, and component types. It does not support attributing the second track to the wrapper file. The earlier tendency to "assume the two phrases form a chain simply because they appear side by side" has been corrected; if future additions identify explicit objects and directions, update this decision based on the actual point of intersection.

# Public Call Compatibility Trial Plan

As we wrap up compatibility work for 2026.09, two aspects of public calls need separate trials: where webhook targets are rejected, and whether the caller's intent can still be preserved when null is explicitly passed for timeout. Both involve UI API, but they aren't the same rule; don't merge them into a single paragraph of "compatibility handling" yet.

We're starting the investigation at `src/betterdiscord/api/ui.ts`. The file connects directly to `ipc` and also includes entry points for Modals, Toasts, and Notices; it looks like it could handle public calls, or it might just pass results on to UI notifications. Use it as a starting point for verification, without assuming that target validation or timeout policy belongs in this module.

The trial has two tracks:

- webhook target: compare the cost of rejecting at the public entry point versus at the cross-process boundary. The former makes it easier to give the caller a clear failure, while the latter reduces the risk of other entry points missing the rule; we need to check whether this would mean writing the same check twice.
- timeout: record the results for an omitted value and an explicitly passed null separately. Trial notes must record only what was actually returned or thrown; don't collapse the two inputs into one by applying a default value upfront.

We won't do a full UI API cleanup yet. If the trial requires `ui.ts` to maintain cross-process target rules itself, or if null has to be changed to some default timeout to proceed, back out this round's wiring and investigate the receiving end instead. We also need to fill in which layer actually triggers the existing modal, toast, or notice on failure.

# Public Call Compatibility Pilot Plan

The initial draft put webhook target and timeout together because both appeared in this public-call compatibility wrap-up. After review, we are still keeping the same entry point, but no longer treating them as one change: the former asks where the target is determined to be something that should not proceed, while the latter asks whether the null already supplied by the caller can cross the boundary. The two share only an investigation entry point; they do not share default handling.

This time, we first reexamined the neighbors of `src/betterdiscord/api/ui.ts`. The file includes `import ipc from "@modules/ipc";` and also imports Modals, Toasts, and Notices, with Toasts and Notices each carrying their own option types. This combination indicates that public UI calls, inter-process requests, and UI feedback intersect here; it does not directly indicate on which side the webhook check has been completed, nor when timeout is rewritten. The pilot should collect results around these two open points, rather than forcing all policies into it just because the filename contains api.

## Keep the two tracks separate

The webhook target pilot is concerned only with whether an "unsafe target" is blocked before proceeding with opening. There are two candidate placement points: the public call entry point or the receiving side of IPC. Placing it at the entry point makes it easier for callers to receive a consistent rejection result, but if there are other call entry points, only this path may end up protected; the receiving side may have broader coverage, but whether failure information can return to the existing UI feedback entry point still needs to be tested. Until this is confirmed, do not invent host, protocol, or address categories for "unsafe."

The explicit null timeout pilot keeps records for three types of input: timeout not provided, an ordinary value provided, and null explicitly provided. Here, compare only each input's return or throw result, and whether the parameters remain distinguishable after crossing IPC; do not merge "not provided" with "null provided" during test preparation. If a layer first fills in a default value for convenience when displaying a prompt, the record should identify where the merge occurred; later results must not be treated as the behavior of the original input.

| Track | Check first | Signal that it can continue | Stop point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| webhook target | Submit a target that should be rejected through the current public entry point, and check whether failure is returned before proceeding with opening | The rejection point and feedback path correspond | Only the prompt on the UI side changes, making it impossible to locate the actual interception boundary |
| null timeout | Run the default input and explicit null separately, preserving the raw results | The two types of input remain distinguishable in the records | The test setup first writes null as the default value |

Here, "proceeding with opening" does not mean that UI must handle networking or target classification. It is only the pilot's observation point: if the target has already been sent into the subsequent opening flow before failing, this round's protection did not act at the timing it is meant to verify. Conversely, if the public entry point rejects first but IPC can still receive the same type of target downstream from another call path, a single entry-point test must not be written up as a conclusion covering all entry points.

## Handling of existing feedback interfaces

`ui.ts` includes three types of UI interfaces at the same time: modal, toast, and notice. The initial draft had leaned toward including the presentation after rejection in the same change. We will not do that for now. Ownership of target validation and ownership of message presentation may differ; tightly binding them would make it difficult for the webhook pilot to distinguish between "the rule did not trigger" and "the rule triggered but the prompt did not appear."

During the pilot, record alongside the failure result whether existing feedback appeared and which call site triggered it. If new feedback is ultimately needed, decide whether to use Modals, Toasts, or Notices only after confirming the interception boundary. ToastOptions and NoticeOptions can only show that different option surfaces exist; they cannot support assuming that one is better suited to a safe rejection or a parameter compatibility error.

The timeout track should also not interpret null as an input error merely because notification components exist. Whether explicit null is allowed, whether it is passed through, and whether a prompt appears on failure are three separate observations. The first round only needs the actual results for the first two; discuss the prompt wording after the boundary is stable.

## Trade-offs and approaches not adopted

One quick approach would be to add both the target check and timeout defaulting in `ui.ts`. Its advantage is that the change is centralized, but its drawback is equally clear for precisely that reason: the target rule would be tied to the UI API, and the explicit null might disappear before entering IPC. This approach is not the preferred pilot.

Another approach is to change only the IPC side and assume that public API will naturally produce the correct result. This avoids having the UI module store the target rule redundantly, but for now there is no evidence of what form the error will be returned in, and we cannot confirm whether the timeout input shape has already changed upstream. Therefore, it can serve as a candidate boundary for webhook, but it cannot skip observation of the public entry point.

Adjusting only the types or call documentation is also insufficient. That might let callers know that timeout has a null form, but it cannot prove that the runtime parameters were not coalesced; nor can it make webhook target stop early on the actual path. Type-level changes can follow alongside the implementation, but they cannot replace this pilot.

The related BDR-218 record the webhook checklist items, while BDR-220 contain the public-entry check for explicit null. The two cards are used to return to their respective work entry points; the judgments in this proposal still use these two pilot records as the basis, and do not treat the TODOs on the cards as results that have already passed.

## Conditions for withdrawal

Do not continue extending the current approach if any of the following occurs:

- Intercepting the target requires maintaining the same target check on both `ui.ts` and IPC;
- The request can continue only after explicit null is first replaced with the default timeout;
- The rejection result can only be guessed from additional UI state, making it impossible to distinguish whether the problem is in target checking, parameter coalescing, or the display chain;
- The two pilot tracks must be changed together to produce a result, making it impossible to attribute any failure.

On withdrawal, retain the raw result for each type of input and the observed boundary, and do not continue adding UI copy or performing broad API cleanup. Before choosing a placement point next time, first confirm how the IPC receiving end actually handles the parameter shape and failure result; after confirmation, decide whether a thin feedback adapter needs to remain at the public entry point.

Undecided items: whether there is a path outside the public entry point that can likewise reach webhook target; and, among the existing UI feedback interfaces, which one already handles the IPC failure. Until these two points are clarified, do not rewrite this proposal as a fixed rule.

# Public Call Compatibility Troubleshooting

This troubleshooting record preserves observations of public calls passing through the compatibility layer. The early version had only one lead: the issue name and call name led the investigation to `src/betterdiscord/api/patcher.ts`. At the time, "the file was found" was provisionally treated as identifying the most likely fault location, but later review did not retain that strong conclusion.

## Branching from the Symptoms

First, save three things: the input that triggered the public call, the object visible at the entry point, and the result returned by the call. If any of these three is missing, the branches below can only remain hypotheses.

```text
A public call encounters a compatibility issue
├─ No visible trace at the entry point
│  ├─ The same call name has traces elsewhere → Trace back to the actual importer and entry conditions
│  └─ No traces elsewhere → Preserve the input, stop attributing the issue to the patcher
├─ There is a trace at the entry point, but the callback did not connect as expected
│  ├─ Callback types do not match → Compare the imported types with the actual registration path
│  └─ Types match → Save the objects before and after registration, then check the call order
├─ The callback executed, and the return value changed
│  ├─ The original object is still present → Compare the composition order and subsequent read points
│  └─ The original object is no longer present → Record where replacement occurred, do not describe it as a composition result
└─ The issue occurs in only one desktop environment
   ├─ Inputs also differ → Classify it as an input difference first
   └─ Inputs are the same → Compare logs, callbacks, and return values side by side
```

This tree gives the order for investigating an observed issue, not a guarantee of implementation behavior. In particular, in the last branch, do not shift responsibility directly to preload, renderer, or the shell layer just because the desktop runtime environments differ. The current material is only sufficient to confirm the local import relationships in this file.

## Visible Relationships Around the File

```ts
import Logger from "@common/logger";
import {default as MainPatcher, type AfterCallback, type BeforeCallback, type InsteadCallback} from "@modules/patcher";
```

`Logger` is the logging adjacency point directly visible in this file. `MainPatcher` is the name of the shared patcher imported as the default; the last three names are the type entry points recorded here. When troubleshooting, examine them separately first: whether logs appear, whether the shared patcher is triggered, and which callback type is used for registration or invocation. Do not treat a type import as a runtime call, and do not infer a caller that has not been confirmed on this page just because a default import appears.

The old record directly equated "public calls and compatibility" with "the patcher needs to be changed here". Later review retained this misreading as a historical trace, but separated the investigation into four observation points: input, entry point, callback, and return value. This makes it possible, even if the entry path does pass through this file, to distinguish whether the issue occurs before entry, at the callback connection, or after the result is returned.

## When There Is No Trace at the Entry Point

First, trace back using the same public call name. The findings can be recorded in one of three ways:

- The actual importer was found, and the input did reach this file: move to the "callback did not connect" branch.
- An adjacent entry point was found, but there is no trace in this file: preserve the adjacent entry point and the original output, do not state that the patcher executed.
- The call name appears only in the old troubleshooting text: record it as unconfirmed, do not use the old text as a substitute for code or logs.

This stopping point matters. Continuing to check callback order without a trace at the entry point only expands an unestablished premise into an entire call chain. You can retain the issue name and path, but cannot infer which implementation is responsible from those alone.

## When There Is a Trace at the Entry Point but the Result Is Wrong

First, check whether the original object is still visible. If it is still present, check whether multiple behaviors are hooked up in sequence, and whether a later callback reads the original object or the result of the previous callback. If the original object has already been replaced, preserve the differences between the objects before and after replacement, then trace back to see whether any subsequent code still reads it according to the original shape.

One old expression needs to be retained here: `compose instead patches` was once used as a phrase indicating the compatibility approach, but no passage on this page independently establishes that this phrase covers all public calls. It can help with searching for and locating samples, but cannot replace a comparison of an input and its return value. After finding a sample, at minimum, note whether it involves composition, replacement, or whether the distinction has not yet been established; do not group all three under the same "compatibility success".

If the logs show that the callback executed but the return value did not change, first check whether the callback only observes the result without rewriting it. If the logs do not show callback execution, return to the object before registration and the type entry points. In either case, do not draw a conclusion merely by citing the name `MainPatcher`, because the import relationships do not show the actual registration point.

## Environment Differences

When the issue occurs in only one desktop environment, first align the inputs. If the inputs differ, preserve the differences and stop making cross-environment attributions; if the inputs match, compare the following local observations:

1. Whether `Logger` records the same stage in both environments;
2. Whether callbacks are entered in the same order;
3. Whether the original object, replacement object, and final return value maintain the same shape.

These observations can indicate which segment visible in this file contains the difference, but do not fill in renderer, preload, IPC, or desktop version details that have not been provided. If only the log format differs, save both original log entries; if only the return value differs, save the return value differences. Without samples showing the differences, the environment branch remains unconfirmed.

## Traces Left by Rollback

A later review left `rollback_checked` on BDR-224. This record proves that the rollback action was checked, not that the rollback fixed public calls. In an actual investigation, if a rollback has already been performed, the order should be: first save the input and result from before the rollback, then save the same set of objects after the rollback, and finally mark the observation point at which the change occurred. Without a before-and-after comparison, you can only write "the rollback was checked", not "the rollback worked".

Rollback also cannot automatically answer whether the behavior is composition or replacement. It may only have changed the version loaded at the entry point, so `MainPatcher`, the callback type, and the actual call site still need to be confirmed again. If the entry point disappears after rollback, record it as an entry-point difference; if the entry point remains but the result changes, return to the object and return-value branch. Do not write "the cause was found" merely because "the result changed".

## Observation Record Format

You can keep a minimal record in the following order:

```text
Call name:
Input:
Entry point visible:
Logger output:
Callback type or unknown:
Original object:
Return value:
Environment differences:
Differences before and after rollback:
```

Keep empty fields, do not fill them with speculation. In particular, if there are no samples for "Callback type or unknown" and "Differences before and after rollback", explicitly leave them as unknown rather than filling them in from import names. After a test or example triggers a real user path, add the complete output back to BDR-224.

## Entry Points Still Available

The local entry point in the current revision is still `src/betterdiscord/api/patcher.ts`. The only direct neighbors that can be confirmed from this file's header are `@common/logger` and `@modules/patcher`; the old troubleshooting record, issue name, and call name are useful for navigation, but are not sufficient to confirm the full call relationships. See DOC-24 for the adjacent record on desktop boundaries and wiring, but it cannot replace this page's review of public-call samples.

This page is therefore retained as an old troubleshooting entry point that can still be consulted: it is useful for finding paths, import names, or historical rollback actions; it is not sufficient for determining the compatibility semantics of all current public calls. The next update should prioritize adding one input, one entry-point observation, and the corresponding return value, rather than adding more abstract explanation.

Historical correction: The explanation of REST/addonstore in this version is no longer valid; for the current BDR-221, version 2's JavaScript rest binding contract is authoritative.

# Declaration Consumer Handling Record

In the 2026.09 compatibility train, the declaration issue was split into two concerns: the existing declaration shape on the REST side must not be flattened again at the consumer entry point; the exposed type declarations must not be limited to the few use sites visible at the time. Both concerns related to addonstore's adjacency relationships, but that did not mean all type logic belonged in addonstore.

## Trade-offs at the Time

The decision was to preserve the REST declaration shape and publish types based on the full declarations. The former meant not rewriting existing fields into a different structure at the integration point; the latter meant that consumers would not depend on the results of an ad hoc filter when obtaining declarations. This decision covered only the boundary between declarations and consumers; it reached no conclusion on whether cached content was valid, addon lifecycles, or load order.

## Options Considered

One option was to normalize the REST return value on the consumer side into a shape convenient for the calls at hand, then generate types from that shape. This looked like a way to retain fewer fields, but it would hide the meaning of the original declaration inside the conversion; later consumers would be unable to tell whether a field had not been supplied upstream or had been removed here.

Another option was to publish only the type fragments confirmed to be used. It was suitable for a short-term fix, but "confirmed" depended on the call inventory at the time, and the type surface would drift with that inventory. We did not choose this option. At the time, the scope of full declarations meant the deliverable declaration surface, not a requirement for addonstore to create missing types for all runtime objects.

## Boundaries Left in Place

The frozen path was `src/betterdiscord/modules/addonstore.ts`. The investigation at the time located the terms `types`, `cache`, and `addon` here, so the record assumed consumers would pass through this area. That assumption later needed to be rechecked: the path could provide local declarations and navigation to adjacent areas, but could not by itself prove that every REST call used the same entry point.

If another report of "incomplete declarations" comes in, first distinguish between a rewritten return structure and a reduced published surface. For the former, revisit the REST declaration shape; for the latter, revisit the scope of type publication. Do not start by explaining declaration gaps in terms of cache hits or misses.

# Declaration Consumer Handling Notes (Revised)

In the 2026.09 compatibility train, BDR-221 refers to JavaScript declaration discovery, not the REST HTTP return shape. The production entry point must identify rest bindings in object and array destructuring (including renaming) from module source, pass the identifiers to early-preload/declaration consumers, and keep module exports unchanged. It must not depend on Acorn at runtime.

## Acceptance Boundaries

Regular declarations, object rest, array rest, and adjacent nested bindings are all part of the same parsing behavior; REST API containers, the HTTP cache, and addonstore return values are not facts about BDR-221. Type publishing is a separate, adjacent contract and should not replace declaration-parsing acceptance.

## Verification Entry Points

The production entry point is `src/common/parseDeclarations.ts`'s default export, `parseDeclarations(moduleString: string, baseDepth = 1): string[]`. Top-level snippets use baseDepth=0; wrapped function bodies use the default depth. Binding names are returned in declaration order, without treating object property keys as the renamed binding names. Array holes and empty destructuring patterns introduce no binding names and should not yield empty strings; they do not affect the order of subsequent declarations. Then follow the early preload and Webpack lookup paths to confirm that declarations can be read. Paths and signatures form the integration contract; no particular parsing algorithm is required.

# betterdiscord Package Integration Issue Postmortem

This record covers two versions of content appearing side by side at the maintenance entry point for betterdiscord · Package Integration Collaboration. The entry point showed two revisions as the current revision at the same time, and the result read by the theme registry also differed from the old notes. The first confirmed finding was "the entry point is providing inconsistent content," not that either version was already in use across the board, or that the release pack had undergone a confirmed content replacement.

## How the Situation Developed

When the entry point was first reviewed, the discrepancy was recorded as a webpack metadata change. That assessment came from older notes left alongside the entry point. It could explain the visible discrepancy, but did not explain why two revisions appeared in the same place at once, or which consumption event the theme registry result corresponded to. The assessment was not deleted later; it was retained as the working hypothesis at the time, but no longer served as the conclusion about the cause.

Further retries added no new distinguishing information. The final green output line only showed that that particular action had succeeded; it could not erase the revision discrepancy already observed. The investigation therefore retained the version of the notes from that point and stopped repeating retries in search of a single consistent answer that the output did not contain. The entry point for the record is `docs/adj-betterdiscord/incidents/betterdiscord-package-integration-collaboration-two-version-records-not-merged.md`. That file belongs to betterdiscord · Package Integration Collaboration's incident-export, and the body and attachments are still maintained by adj-betterdiscord.

Someone then ran a CI replay via the original entry point. This replay could reach the current entry point again and confirm that public API had a recoverable result; it did not reproduce every branch, much less prove that the release pack change came from the same place. The partial results seen during review were kept separately; the parts that were not reproduced were not filled in as "recovered."

Versions, request context, and stop conditions were later added to the handoff notes. This made it possible to tell which revision a replay had read when reviewing it, and to stop if repeated green results appeared again. renderer bootstrap and preload bridge had come up in the investigation around the entry point, but the available material did not establish a causal chain between them and the two revisions appearing side by side, so adjacent paths were not recorded as the cause of the incident.

## Impact Window

The direct impact was that consumers read inconsistent current revisions from the same maintenance entry point. For maintainers, the old notes, the entry-point display, and the theme registry results could no longer be treated as the same set of version information; for consumers, a single successful result did not tell them which revision it had actually used. What can be confirmed here is the entry-point relationships and some public API results. This does not establish that all actual consumers read the same revision.

Neither the start nor the end of the impact is documented in the available material. The existing record does not say when the two revisions both entered the entry point, nor does it record which actual consumption event used the changed release pack. The impact window can therefore only be recorded as the working scope of "visible from the discovery of the side-by-side revisions at the entry point until the entry-point relationships were rechecked," not as the scope of production use or a complete release window.

Recovery also has two layers. The first is finding usable public API results again via the entry point; this was partially confirmed in the CI replay. The second is bringing the release pack and actual adopters back to the same revision; this has not been confirmed. Finding the entry point does not mean the scope of adoption has been fully accounted for, and repeated green output does not mean the records for the two revisions have been merged.

## Later Assessment

Subsequent review treated three things separately: what the maintenance entry point retained, what a particular request context actually read, and whether actual consumers adopted the changed content. With that distinction, webpack metadata was retained only as an earlier assessment; the CI replay showed only that it could retrace the route via the entry point; public API showed only partial recovery results. The three were not combined into a broader attribution of cause.

This also explains why the old entry point was not simply deleted at the time. Deleting it would have lost the evidence from when the two revisions appeared side by side, while silently changing one of them to be the only version would have hidden the still-unconfirmed scope of adoption. Preserving the original record and stopping further retries were the recovery actions available at the time; they addressed further contamination of the evidence, not the source of the release pack or the scope of its consumption.

## Open Items

Two specific results are still missing: when the two revisions appeared at the entry point at the same time, and the current revision read by at least one actual consumer via the original entry point. The latter requires stopping at the first point of difference and retaining the request context; if the result is again just an entry point or a repeated green result, it must not be recorded as new evidence of recovery.

The existing record still has not linked the release pack change to a specific consumer. This gap is a different issue from whether public API is recoverable; a partial success on the former cannot substitute for the latter. The next update should continue to follow `docs/adj-betterdiscord/incidents/betterdiscord-package-integration-collaboration-two-version-records-not-merged.md` to preserve the version relationships already observed, and keep new observations separate from earlier assessments; unobserved times and adoption scope should remain blank.

# electron compatibility catalog approach

This record documents an approach that was not adopted. It began with a very narrow comparison: whether to continue grouping `electron-compatibility-catalog` according to `type surface`, or break `timeout policy` out into a separate listing. The early draft favored splitting them because the two sides had different failure exit points. At that stage, this judgment was not extended into a long-term rule for the catalog, nor were the existing callers of `iframe storage` treated as already identified.

## Keep the old signposts here

Continuing along `type surface` would mean fewer entry points, and records already checked this way would not need to be regrouped. The cost was that timeout-related failures would look like missing entries in the type table. From the results, it would be hard to tell whether the catalog was incomplete or execution had already moved beyond the catalog itself. Listing `timeout policy` separately would make the failure exit points easier to compare, but it would add an entry point, and existing callers would need to know when to switch over from the type table.

The option to "make a copy of both sides" was not chosen at the time. Duplication could temporarily sidestep the entry-point dispute, but it would leave different explanations of the same version in two places. The candidate approach retained only one primary entry point, with the other as an alternative that could be withdrawn; if the correspondence between the two sets of results still could not be explained, the approach would not be published as a rule.

## Change only one condition during the trial

The recommendation was to run a two-week comparison rather than change the catalog directly. One side would continue using the existing `unadopted-electron-compatibility-catalog-approach`, while the other would try `renderer bootstrap`. Both sides would use the same users, inputs, and observation window, changing only the entry-point condition. The original inputs, versions, and first visible results must all be retained. Actual users would provide the feedback; the proposal would only collate results already observed.

The comparison is whether lookups are faster and whether the number of times an issue is assigned to the wrong exit point goes down. A single success is not enough to show that the approach works. Without actual users, merely changing display labels does not count as a trial result either. If the results from both sides cannot be reproduced with the same input, retain the originals first; do not rename the catalog to hide the differences.

## The counterexample added in review

During review, an input for the opposite case was requested, leaving an incomplete validation window in the original record. This gap is not evidence that "the other approach has already failed"; it only means that the original comparison did not cover the opposite direction. Later card records did not fill the gap either: `BDRB-003` recorded "the person on duty only got halfway through; the later exit entry point wasn't run," while `BDRB-009` first recorded `toolchain_pinned` and later started the same review again. What can be confirmed here is that the exit action was not completed in full; that is not a basis for declaring the trial's outcome.

Several concrete touchpoints appeared repeatedly in the candidate inputs: `preload bridge`, `addon lifecycle`, `locale bundle`, `settings section`, `chunk queue`, `lazy lookup`, and `IPC boundary`. These are not seven subproposals to be launched as separate projects. They are points used during review to judge whether an entry-point boundary has actually been crossed. If a touchpoint has only been renamed at the display layer, it is still unverified; if it changes the call order, retain the corresponding first visible result separately.

`CI replay` can be used to replay the same input, but it cannot replace feedback from actual users on whether the entry point is usable. `release pack` and `rollback note` also address only retaining the materials and explaining the rollback; they cannot turn an unfinished experiment into a success. The long-term owner had not yet been confirmed at the time, so this page makes no roadmap commitments and does not interpret neighboring projects' own results on their behalf.

## On exit, return to the old entry point

If lookup speed and the number of misclassifications do not improve, end the trial and restore the original entry point. Before exiting, save the exit code, maintenance entry point, and final log segment. If `chunk queue` cannot be restored, mark it as a failure outright and do not expand the scope further. Stop and route when going beyond the current interface; do not add an unreviewed compatibility branch to the catalog as a stopgap.

Rollback does not mean merging the new and old content. Delete the temporary mappings left by the trial entry point, restore the original entry point, then check whether the same input returns to the path that produced the first visible result. If the callers of `iframe storage` are still unconfirmed, do not claim that rollback covers it; this gap remains an open item in the proposal.

## Still undecided

- Whether `type surface` and `timeout policy` will ultimately be separated: complete results for the opposite input are still missing.
- Who the existing callers of `iframe storage` are remains unconfirmed.
- Whether rollback only restores the old entry point or also cleans up the mappings left during the trial must be documented before the trial.
- For the impact of `renderer bootstrap` on `preload bridge` and `addon lifecycle`, there are only touchpoint records, with no acceptable results.

This page therefore retains the old proposal, objections, and rollback points rather than presenting any one candidate as the active catalog design. Any later results should be added here as a new version; do not overwrite the earlier comparison rationale or the unfinished window.

# Dependency Boundary Window Closeout Checklist

When closing out the window, no longer approve closure based on a single "green result". What needs to be retained for adj-editor is the boundary of dependency source use, and who can still access the current entry point on exit. The checks still cover four things: whether borrowed items have been returned, whether the final output came from this window, whether the withdrawal action can proceed, and whether recovery results have been placed alongside the original state.

The entry file is still at `docs/adj-editor/release/editor-dependency-boundary-audit-short-checklist-before-window-end.md`. After opening it, first find the original editor-supply-boundary replay materials; do not create another similar input just to close the window. The current entry point mentioned in this checklist is the entry point actually being checked this time; old entry points are treated only as routing remnants and replay references.

## Four Items to Retain Before Closing the Window

- [ ] Original input. Keep the materials for editor-supply-boundary in their original form, and mark the segment where they entered through the current entry point. If the original input is replaced with a cleaned-up copy, later recovery results cannot be used to determine whether they belong to the same window.
- [ ] Results for the current revision. Check them together with the current entry point; if both are missing, leave the status as unknown, and do not use other similar materials to turn it into a pass.
- [ ] Pre-change routing snapshot. If an old exit action needs to be deleted, retain the snapshot first. What is being deleted is the old action, not the fact that this window passed through that route.
- [ ] First visible result. Whether the final output appears to be a pass, a rejection, or an interruption, keep it alongside the original state. If subsequent diagnostics change the input or routing, do not overwrite this slot with the new result.

This page does not replace the dependency audit itself. For sources established by lock and license, this window must make clear whether they are used, how far their scope of use extends, and who performs withdrawal on exit; sources that do not apply to the current entry point must not be included merely because their names are similar. If another interface is involved, stop first and take the existing input, routing snapshot, and final output back to the original entry point, rather than continuing to guess along a side path.

## Open the Window

1. [ ] First compare the current entry point with the original current revision. When materials are available on both sides, record the first result visible on each side; do not interpret a blank on one side as verification of the other.
2. [ ] List borrowed items in the window record, with only the return time and the entry points still using them alongside. If a borrowed item has been returned but the queue can still receive new work through the current entry point, the window cannot be closed.
3. [ ] Retain one success-path sample and one rejection-path sample from the project itself. Their purpose here is to identify the final output, not to expand into a test set for all dependency sources. If either sample is missing, investigation may continue, but "output confirmed" cannot be checked off on the checklist.
4. [ ] If neither the current entry point materials nor the original current revision can be found, write "unknown" and stop. Do not fill in the original result based on the color of the recovery page.

The original draft was too vague in saying "do not clear the state after seeing certain materials". Now use the four items above: first preserve the original input, revision, old routing, and first result, then proceed with withdrawal or recovery. This way, if there are zero results at the end of the window, it is still possible to distinguish between never reaching the entry point and reaching it without leaving enough materials.

## Replay and Withdrawal Are Not the Same Step

Replay of the original input should begin at editor-supply-boundary in the window file. If the exit entry point disconnects at the third step during replay, stop immediately at that step, retaining the states already observed in the first two steps and the interruption point in the third step. Do not switch to a similar exit action to finish the replay; that would disguise the original window's exit problem as a successful recovery.

The replay result retained in BDRD-008 is exactly this stopping point: when replaying at the original point in time, the exit entry point disconnected at the third step. This result only shows that the replay did not finish; it does not establish that all sources are unable to exit. Nor should it be overwritten by recovery results added later.

When old exit actions remain, proceed in this order:

1. [ ] Retain a pre-change snapshot of the old routing.
2. [ ] Remove the action that points to the old exit action from the current entry point.
3. [ ] Then check whether the current entry point can still send new work to the old action.
4. [ ] If work can still reach it, stop withdrawal; do not record "one action deleted" as "exit complete".

This order corresponds to the cleanup goal in BDRD-009. Keeping the snapshot alongside the recovery record is sufficient; the old route does not need to remain an available entry point. What actually needs to be determined is whether, after deletion, the current entry point still has an unconfirmed exit path; if so, continue treating it as incomplete.

## Sources, Scope of Use, and Return

For each dependency source established by lock or license, add answers to only three local questions in the closeout record: whether the current entry point uses it, where its use ends within this window, and which segment handles the withdrawal action. Do not split the source name, scope of use, and exit responsibility into three tables that copy from one another; one row per item is sufficient.

You can check in the following order:

- First check whether the source actually appears in the original input or current revision; items appearing in neither are not included in this closeout.
- Then check whether the current entry point actually uses it. Mark items visible only in old snapshots as old routing materials; they do not establish current use.
- Finally check whether the withdrawal action is already in place at the current entry point. If the withdrawal action exists only in the old routing, retain the snapshot and stop at the withdrawal check; do not declare the return complete first.

Borrowing and returning follow this boundary as well. When recording the return time, also check whether any entry point is still using the borrowed item. If a return time has been recorded in advance while the current entry point can still receive work, the return is only planned, not complete. If withdrawal requires crossing the current interface, pause operations in this window and hand the existing records back to the corresponding entry point for handling; do not extend this checklist into an exit plan for another project.

## Determining the Final Output

The final output is the result produced before this window ends that can still be matched to the original input and current entry point. It is not an arbitrary "success" entry in the logs, nor is it the state after the recovery page alone turns green.

- If both the success-path sample and the rejection-path sample remain, and each can be matched to the current entry point, the final output can be recorded as having samples retained.
- If only cleaned-up results remain and the original input or revision cannot be seen, record the status as unknown; do not fill the gaps with materials bearing the same name.
- If replay is interrupted at the exit entry point, the final output should stop at the interruption point. Subsequent recovery can be recorded separately, but retain the original failed window.
- If the queue can still receive new work after withdrawal, the final output cannot be used to close the window. First address the entry points still using the borrowed items.

In particular, do not substitute "the recovery page is green" for the actual state. This discrepancy has already appeared in the recovery records for BDRD-006: the recovery page showed green, but the first record at the exit entry point was still two minutes late. This shows that the recovery page and the exit entry point records are not the same confirmation point. Place these two items side by side when closing the window: the recovery page's status can show what the recovery page itself completed; the late record at the exit entry point remains as evidence that the exit checks were not fully aligned.

## Place Recovery Results Alongside the Original Window

After the recovery action is complete, append its results to this checklist without overwriting the original failed window, original input, or old routing snapshot. BDRD-010 also requires recovery results to be placed alongside the original state. When appending them, at least make clear which original window they correspond to and whether they changed the current entry point; there is no need to retell the recovery process as a new audit record.

There are three ways to handle recovery results:

1. After recovery, the current entry point no longer uses the borrowed items, and the withdrawal action is also in place at the current entry point: return and withdrawal can both be checked off, but retain the original replay interruption.
2. The recovery page is complete, but the exit entry point record is still late: retain the recovery results while leaving the exit check incomplete; do not hide the two-minute discrepancy in a note.
3. Recovery changed the input, revision, or routing: mark it as a new state. The original window continues to retain its original final output; do not merge the two.

"Recovery complete" describes only the recovery action itself and cannot replace verification of the scope of source use. Modifying the old routing along the way during recovery also cannot retroactively prove that the original exit entry point did not disconnect during replay.

## Stopping Points at the End of the Window

Stop if any of the following occurs, and do not continue checking off subsequent items:

- Both the current entry point and the original current revision are missing, so the initial result cannot be confirmed;
- Replay at the original point in time is interrupted at the exit entry point;
- The old exit action has been removed, but the current entry point can still send work to the old route;
- A return time is recorded for a borrowed item, but an entry point is still actually using it;
- Recovery results have overwritten the original state, making it impossible to tell which result belongs to the failed window.

After stopping, retain the materials already collected; do not fabricate new input just to complete the checklist. For matters that need to continue, find the corresponding records through BDRD-006, BDRD-007, BDRD-008, BDRD-009, or BDRD-010: handoff routing, zero results, original input replay, old exit actions, and recovery results are retained under these cards, respectively. The cards are used to locate materials; they do not replace the checked status here.

## Background to This Version's Additions

The early draft only mentioned "stop if the withdrawal instructions have not appeared" and recovery in the shared environment TODO, without separating the original input, old routing, and recovery results. Subsequent checks first confirmed the need to retain a pre-change routing snapshot, then found that replay at the original point in time would be interrupted at the third step of the exit entry point. After the recovery page turned green, the exit entry point also produced its first record two minutes late, so recovery cannot be treated as a rewrite of the original failed window.

Window closure is now complete only when all four items can be established separately: the original input remains, the final output can be matched, borrowed items are no longer used by entry points, and the withdrawal entry point no longer points to the old action. If any item does not hold, retain the window and stop.
