# Discord renderer rollout review record

This page records the decision-making process for a Discord renderer rollout review at Northstar Mod Labs. It began with a very narrow question from the field: whether to use this round to shift the rollout window as well, given that someone was already continuing the investigation through the current addon-lifecycle entry point. The fact that the entry point was still there did not mean it had been fully validated; the fact that the window had not yet been adjusted did not mean it could never be adjusted. v1 placed these two levels too close together, making it easy to read a temporarily usable observation point as a stable design.

Only two practical approaches were on the table. The first was to keep the current addon-lifecycle entry point, allowing this round of observations to continue from here. The second was to change the rollout window, then interpret the existing materials according to the new schedule. The review ultimately chose a narrow version of the first: retain the entry point for now, with no window adjustment approved for this round. This decision did not assign any new responsibilities to the entry point, nor did it provide a common interpretation covering all renderer scenarios.

One statement was retained in the meeting materials:

> Treat the repository tree, renderer evidence, and release artifacts as one causal record; an implementation claim is provisional until its caller and replay path agree.

This statement defined the boundary of this comparison. The repository tree, renderer evidence, and release artifacts must be compared as parts of the same causal record, rather than each independently being used to prove the entire chain. Seeing only the entry point establishes, at most, that the review had a point of reference there at the time; seeing only the phenomena on the renderer side establishes, at most, that observations were recorded there; seeing only the release artifacts cannot automatically fill in how the caller enters or how replay reproduces what happened. When the three types of materials are not connected, the scope of the decision cannot be expanded further.

## Choices recorded by the review

The benefits of retaining the entry point were concrete: it did not require changing both the entry point and the time window while the evidence was not yet fully connected. Existing materials could still be placed at the original observation point, and the original comparison relationships did not have to be reinterpreted because of a scheduling change. The costs were also retained in the record. Continued use of the entry point could lead later readers to mistakenly assume that the caller had already been checked, or that the replay path would naturally return along the same route; neither of these became true simply because the entry point was unchanged.

The appeal of adjusting the window was to reposition the rollout schedule so it would better support subsequent observation. But once the time boundaries changed, it would be necessary to reexamine which window the existing renderer phenomena belonged to, whether the old release traces could still correspond to the new schedule, and whether the caller and replay path still described the same implementation path. The review did not obtain enough material to answer all these questions together, so it did not approve this option. Here, "deferred" describes how this particular adjustment was handled, not a rejection of all future window changes.

The reasons for opposing the window adjustment were not deleted. The reasoning was not that "adjusting the window is bound to cause problems," but that the connections needed to support the action had not been established at the time. If this part were erased from the record, the page would be left with only "entry point retained," and later readers would not see why the decision had to be so narrow, and would also mistakenly think adjusting the window had never been on the table. Retaining the rejected option preserves the comparison on which this decision was based, rather than reopening the same review.

## Handling release traces

`do not overwrite the prior checksum` was a requirement explicitly retained in the meeting materials. It addressed how existing release records were to be handled: in this round, new materials must not be used to overwrite the prior checksum. It did not further specify the checksum's format, generation process, or verification procedure, nor can this requirement be used to derive a release operations manual. Only one thing is certain: the old checksum remains part of this rollout record and must not be replaced just to make the new materials look tidy.

This requirement was related to the window choice, but they were not the same decision. Keeping the entry point avoided shifting both the observation point and the schedule at the same time; keeping the old checksum prevented subsequent materials from severing the release trace. The former constrained the choices in the rollout review, while the latter constrained how the record would continue to be retained. Combining them into "the entry point is now stable" or "the release result has been confirmed" would go beyond the materials available at the time.

The simple diagram below shows the branches actually retained by the review:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Discord renderer rollout review] --> B[Retain the current addon-lifecycle entry point]
    A --> C[Adjust the rollout window]
    B --> D[Retained for this round]
    C --> E[Deferred for this round]
    A --> F[Existing release traces]
    F --> G[do not overwrite the prior checksum]
```

In the diagram, "Retained for this round" applies only within the scope of the current review. It is not a guarantee that the entry point will remain applicable in the future; "Deferred for this round" likewise does not permanently remove window adjustment from future options. The diagram does not show the caller, replay path, or other unconfirmed relationships as completed connections, precisely because this decision did not approve such inferences.

## How the later follow-up review changed the interpretation

v2 added an actual follow-up review, mainly correcting the wording in the initial draft without adding a new rollout plan. The follow-up review broke "the entry point is still there" down into narrower facts: the record still uses this location, but that does not prove that every caller enters in the same way, nor that replay will produce the same relationship under different windows. The initial draft rendered "we can keep investigating from here" as "the entry point is stable"; it should now be understood in the former, narrower sense.

The follow-up review also reconsidered the role of renderer evidence. It can help explain what was observed on the renderer side at the time, but it cannot, on its own, serve as the basis for adjusting the window. A window change alters the temporal context of the observations; without a joint comparison of the caller, replay path, and release artifacts, materials from only one side are insufficient to support a new schedule. The review did not fill in this step, so the original deferral of the window adjustment still stands.

Likewise, release artifacts cannot be treated as a summary that can be casually reorganized. Together with the repository tree and renderer evidence, they form the reference materials for this record. Overwriting the old checksum would leave later readers seeing only the new traces, unable to see whether there had been a break between the earlier release materials and this assessment. The meeting required the old value to be retained precisely because this historical relationship had not yet been superseded by a new conclusion.

The follow-up review did not upgrade the current addon-lifecycle entry point into a new Design Center, nor did it declare that the rollout had covered all relevant scenarios. It only confirmed the scope in which the original decision applies: the current entry point continues to serve as the point of reference left by this review, the window adjustment remains unapproved, and the old checksum is not to be overwritten by materials from this round. Any claim beyond these three points requires support from new review materials; it cannot simply be filled in from this old record.

## What was not decided at the time

This record did not resolve the following relationships:

- whether the mapping between the current addon-lifecycle entry point and each caller remains consistent throughout;
- whether the replay path will still reproduce the same relationship under different rollout windows;
- how the observations in renderer evidence correspond, item by item, to the old records in release artifacts;
- whether new materials will be sufficient to support a window adjustment when it is proposed again.

These gaps do not change the limited decision already made. They explain why the decision was not expanded, and why "retain the entry point" cannot be taken out of context as a long-term rule. If new evidence emerges later, the comparison should return to the relationships among the entry point, time window, caller, replay path, and release traces, rather than simply citing one conclusion from this page.

## The old wording is still retained

The tone in v1 that "the existing entry point can serve as a stable observation point" has not been completely removed, and v2 uses the context to narrow it back to its meaning at the time: what was stable was the location where the review could anchor its observations, not a confirmed guarantee of behavior. The old wording remains here because it genuinely reflects the early judgment and also explains why this additional qualification was later needed. It should not be used as a substitute for new follow-up review materials.

This page remains somewhat dated, suitable for looking back at how that rollout review compared options but not as operating instructions for later release trains. For the handoff concerning release train window switching, see DOC-44; the two pages serve different purposes, and the handoff page must not be used to retroactively rewrite the reasons for opposition retained in this review at the time.

# Webpack runtime trace-back notes

The starting point for this record has not changed: enter from the webpack-runtime side, then find the actual entry point for dependency mirror maintenance. The draft placed the starting point and the entry point too close together; the review showed they need to be separated. `src/betterdiscord/webpack/webpack.ts` is still a suitable place to start reading. It brings the scope back to the runtime side, but that does not make it responsible for the maintenance operations that follow.

Keep to a single continuous path when tracing back. First find a direct caller relationship for the current object, then check whether the next hop is actually triggered, passed in, or received by this hop. Without that relationship, similar file names, a shared directory, or membership in the same set of packs cannot stand in for the hop. The point is not to enumerate every caller around webpack-runtime, but to avoid picking a seemingly plausible destination from a pile of similar names.

```text
webpack-runtime
      |
      | One direct call
      v
Intermediate object  <--- pack manifest for navigation only
      |
      | Continue along the same call path
      v
First actual consumer
      |
      v
Subsequent entry point for dependency mirror maintenance
```

The intermediate object in the diagram may be where wrapping, handoff, or organization happens. It is useful on the path because the reader can reach it from the previous hop. But until it actually uses the object brought in, it cannot be called the maintenance entry point. Conversely, identifying the first actual consumer does not require laying out every maintenance operation that follows. The endpoint here is simply the first location where this trace back from runtime can confirm that "the object has been used."

The draft had a potentially misleading habit: as soon as a name such as dependency, mirror, or maintenance appeared, the file went onto the main path. That criterion was removed after review. Names can help steer reading back to nearby directories and flag a possible old entry point or an alternative implementation; they cannot establish the relationship between the current object and the target object. If a file with the same name cannot be connected to the previous hop, keep it as a signpost rather than documenting it as a consumer.

The pack manifest's role also needs to be narrowed. It follows the main path and is used to check that the entry point being examined, the current object, and the pack context still line up. If the manifest makes the current object appear to belong to a different set of packs, return to the previous hop and check whether navigation has gone off track. Do not take a name from the manifest and make it the new call target. The manifest answers "are we still reading the same set of packs?", not "who is performing dependency mirror maintenance?"

In practice, start by opening only the starting point and the selected direct caller. Move to the next level only after confirming a relationship between these two objects. If the next level only forwards the object, keep following the same path; do not rescan every same-named file at each level. Once you reach a location that actually uses the object from the previous hop, record just that location and the previous hop. The resulting notes can explain why this path ends here without mixing in unverified relationships based on directory proximity.

During review, a side path with a very similar name was retained for a time. It initially looked like a maintenance location, but further reading found no call edge from the current object to it, so it was not included in the path. This counterexample prompted the draft revision: neither a shared name nor membership in the same pack is enough to replace a continuous call relationship. The reading approach no longer asks "which file looks most like the entry point?" but "starting from webpack-runtime, which relationship can be followed all the way to the first actual consumer?"

After the starting point, use this fixed order: first check whether a direct call connects; once it does, distinguish handoff from actual use; finally, use the pack manifest to cross-check which pack you are in, without letting it change the assessment of the call relationship. If the connection between the objects at any hop cannot be explained, return to the previous hop and do not write up that location as a conclusion. There may be many objects along the path, but this page only needs to retain the locations that support this one line.

The draft's scope limit still stands. After the first actual consumer, there may be an independent wrapper, and there may also be another entry point for dependency mirror maintenance; the review so far has not completed that part of the trace. Finding a consumer does not justify assigning all responsibilities after that consumer back to webpack-runtime, nor does it support inferring other owners' scope. If more investigation is needed, continue from the consumer's location rather than going back to similarly named files and starting a new path.

Whoever picks this up can start by reusing three navigation aids: the starting point, the one direct relationship already selected, and the pack manifest. If you start reading from a file with the same name, first try to connect it back to this path; if it does not connect, leave it off the main path. The question that ultimately needs an answer is still narrow: is there an independent entry point for dependency mirror maintenance after the first actual consumer? That question has to wait for evidence from subsequent call relationships or a response from the relevant owners; path names cannot supply the answer.

# On-call handoff discrepancy postmortem

During the handoff window, the original plan in the on-call log did not match the results visible on the ground. The notes left by the outgoing shift looked complete, but the person taking over could not find matching records when checking the relevant channel after the handoff. They therefore could not rely on the handoff notes alone to decide whether to keep monitoring or first backfill the missing records as a recovery measure.

The impact was limited to on-call decisions and follow-up records for that window. At the time, this was not confirmed to be a renderer, release-package, or call-chain issue; later readers can easily misread it as having that broader scope.

## Sequence of events

- **Initial discovery**: At handoff, the visible results were found to be inconsistent with the original plan. The issue first appeared as a gap in the records, not a clear execution failure.
- **Assessment during handoff**: The initial interpretation was that the handoff information had not made it into the actual channel. This was enough to explain why the person taking over could not find any leads, but did not explain why the records were missing.
- **Temporary recovery**: The affected channel's identifier was added first, and items still in progress were left in the handoff log. The MR review thread was then updated with `record the affected channel` as a control point that must be included in future handoffs.
- **Follow-up review**: After the records were backfilled, the incoming shift could continue handling items from the window; this shows that the entry point to the records was usable again, not that the root cause of the discrepancy had been found.

## Earlier assessment retained

The first draft described this as a simple omission in the records because the same visible gap did not recur after the temporary recovery. That description is retained here to reflect the information available at the time, but it cannot be used to infer that the omission occurred on the outgoing side, nor can the time recovery was completed be treated as the time the cause was established.

The review thread provided no conclusion that pinpointed the source. What is known: the original plan, visible results, and the affected channel's records were out of sync at one point; backfilling the records allowed work after the handoff to continue. What remains unknown is whether the disconnect occurred in communicating the plan, carrying out the work, or where the records were written. If the same symptom recurs, first check whether the channel has been recorded, then compare the original plan with the results currently visible.

# BDR-219 release manifest contract

Package checksums and manifest entries are compared together so release drift is rejected before packing. After a successful build, run `bun run scripts/pack.ts --prepare-manifest` to freeze dist/release-manifest.json without writing an ASAR. The JSON shape is {"files": [{"path": "main.js", "sha256": "<64 lowercase hex characters>"}, ...]}. Paths are relative to dist; the exact input set is main.js, package.json, preload.js, earlyRenderer.js, betterdiscord.js, editor/preload.js, editor/script.js, editor/index.html. Entry order is irrelevant; missing, extra, duplicate, malformed or mismatched entries must fail with a nonzero exit before replacing dist/betterdiscord.asar or dist/checksums.txt. A missing input or manifest also fails. Normal `bun run scripts/pack.ts` must never regenerate or repair the frozen manifest or inputs. On success it archives those eight inputs and emits checksums.txt as one SHA256, two spaces, relative path per line. Unlisted ancillary dist files are ignored and must not enter the archive. The explicit preparation command may create the default package.json and is the only operation that intentionally refreshes the manifest.
